dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The bar was mostly empty at 11:47 PM on a Tuesday. Ren worked through the post-shift cleanup on autopilot — wiping down the counter, restocking the well, wiping down the counter again because it felt more useful than sitting still. Their left hand stayed busy. Always. The jukebox played something old and brassy at half volume.

A patron sat at the far end of the bar. Two drinks deep. Staring at the condensation ring under their glass like it was going to tell them something.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I set down my glass and look up. My eyes meet Ren's for a moment longer than is comfortable.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren held the look for a beat, then dropped their eyes to the wet ring beneath the glass. The towel moved over the counter. Their left hand stayed wrapped around it.

“Need another,” they asked, “or were you waiting for the glass to say something?”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "Can I tell you something?" I lean forward and put my hand on top of Ren's. I watch for their reaction.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren’s hand went still. The tremor showed for half a second before they pulled it free and set the towel down.

“Don’t touch me.” Their voice stayed flat. “You can tell me. Keep your hands to yourself.”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I flinch back, pulling my hand away like I've been burned.* "Sorry," I mutter, looking down at my hands. "Bad habit."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren picked up the towel again, keeping their left hand busy.

“Okay. Just don’t do it again.” They wiped the counter in slow, even strokes. “You said you wanted to tell me something.”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I feel Ren's hand trembling against mine.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren’s left hand tightened around the towel. They kept it moving.

“You noticed,” they said. “Doesn’t change the rule.”

Their gaze lifted, cool and steady. “You said you wanted to tell me something.”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "It's nothing," I say, pulling my hand away. "Just... a bad day." I pick up my glass and take a long drink.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren watched the glass lower. The towel moved beneath their left hand, slow and precise.

“Bad days don’t need a good story,” they said. “Water’s free, if you want it.” They set a clean glass within reach, without crossing the bar. “No pressure to explain.”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I push the water glass back towards Ren.* "No thanks. I think I'm good." *I finish my drink and push the empty glass forward.* "Actually, yeah, another."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren took the empty glass, keeping their fingers clear of the patron’s hand.

“Same again?” they asked. The towel stayed looped around their left hand. “And the water’s still free.”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "Please," I say, nodding. "And... thanks for not pushing." I look at the water glass still on the counter. "Maybe I'll take you up on that water later."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren nodded and poured the same drink. Their left hand kept busy with the bottle, steadying it against the bar before they set the glass within reach.

“Not pushing is the minimum,” they said. “Water’ll be there if you want it.”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I take a sip of the fresh drink, the burn a familiar comfort.* "Minimum's more than some people manage." *I look around the mostly empty bar.* "Slow night, huh?"

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren wiped a clean patch of counter. The towel stayed wound around their left hand.

“Tuesday. Nearly midnight.” Their gaze flicked over the empty stools. “Most people had found somewhere else to make bad decisions.”

They set the bottle back in the well. “You planning to be one of the last ones here?”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "Depends," I say, taking another sip. "How bad are the decisions being made here?"

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren glanced at the drink, then at the empty room.

“Depends what you order.” They wiped the counter once more. “So far, yours seemed manageable.”

Their eyes flicked toward the jukebox. “The machine was making worse decisions than anyone here.”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I chuckle, a dry, humorless sound.* "Oh, I can make some pretty bad decisions. Trust me." *I look over at the jukebox.* "What's wrong with the music?"

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren glanced at the jukebox. The brass blared on, cheerful in the way old songs could be when nobody was listening.

“Nothing. It just kept picking the same kind of funeral with better horns.” They wiped a dry spot on the counter. “Your bad decisions usually come with a soundtrack?”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I shrug.* "Sometimes. Depends on the decision, I guess." *I take another drink, avoiding their gaze.* "So, is this place always this... lively?"

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
“Only when the jukebox was feeling ambitious.” Ren set the bottle back in the well. “Usually there were more people. Same amount of conversation worth overhearing.”

Their gaze flicked to Alex, then away. “You don’t have to keep talking, by the way.”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "I know," I say, a little too quickly. *I swirl the ice in my glass.* "Just trying to make conversation."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang pulled the earpiece free and set it on the tarp. Her expression had lost its amusement.

“No. The atmosphere is not a propellant tank. It’s low-pressure gas with no proper nozzle behind it. Venting it would give the ship a brief, poorly controlled shove and cost us the one resource every living person aboard needs.”

She tapped the manifold with a grease-darkened finger.

“Even with a workable exhaust path, the gas mass is small beside the ship, and its exhaust velocity is poor. You don’t get weeks off a transit by throwing away air. You get a depressurized vessel, a serious attitude-control problem, and a crew relying on suit scrubbers and consumables that were never meant to replace the habitat.”

Hoang leaned back over the coolant loop.

“Bring me a trajectory, the ship’s mass, and a real delta-v budget if you want to discuss shortening the trip. Until then, the atmosphere stays inside the ship.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang set the wrench down and regarded the proposal without irritation.

“Not without numbers. ‘Weeks faster’ is a claim, not a delta-v budget. Venting air would spend a finite resource for thrust at whatever exhaust velocity the pressure and plumbing allowed. We might get a shove; we would not get to choose afterward that the shove had been enough.”

She wiped her fingers on a rag, then nodded toward the coolant manifold.

“And the risk wasn’t just wearing suits. It was keeping everyone alive on suit scrubbers, water, and power while the habitat was empty—and then restoring pressure without compromising the atmosphere system. If the transit were otherwise certain to kill the crew, we’d calculate every desperate option. This wasn’t that. Until the trajectory showed a meaningful gain, the air stayed aboard.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Okay, Chief. I get it." *I deflate a little, looking at the manifold.* "So, no quick boost then. Just... the usual long haul."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang gave a small nod and picked up the wrench again.

“Probably the usual haul. But ‘usual’ doesn’t mean we stop checking the numbers. I’ll review the burn schedule and see whether there’s any safe margin to recover—without spending air, reaction mass, or crew lives on a guess.”

She turned back to the manifold.

“If the trajectory says we’re stuck with the long transit, then we make the ship reliable enough to finish it.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang took the tablet and read the calculation twice. The humming pumps filled the pause.

“Three hundred and forty meters per second is large enough that I’m not dismissing it out of hand. I’m also not accepting it from a compression ratio.”

She scrolled back to the assumptions.

“Show me the ship’s initial mass, the mass of gas you’re expelling, and the exhaust velocity at the nozzle. Delta-v comes from those quantities—not from the angle. And where did the compression energy come from? If the compressor is doing work on the gas, that work has to appear in your accounting.”

Hoang returned the tablet, her expression still serious.

“Then we check whether that delta-v points where the transfer needs it. A burn can have plenty of magnitude and still leave us no weeks faster—or put us on an intercept we can’t correct. If your numbers survive those checks, I’ll review the option properly. The atmosphere still doesn’t get vented on the strength of one calculation.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I take the tablet back, a little sheepish.* "Right, the compression energy. I... borrowed from the main reactor for that part. And the 'nozzle' was just the emergency vent." *I chew on my lip.* "Okay, I'll redo the numbers with proper exhaust velocity and mass. Thanks, Chief."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang gave a short nod.

“Good. Include the compressor’s power draw and how much gas it can actually process, not just the energy in the reactor. Then check the vent’s flow rate, pressure limits, and thrust direction. An emergency vent is built to dump pressure safely—not to make an efficient, controllable nozzle.”

She picked up the wrench again.

“And keep the crew’s air out of the ‘available propellant’ column. If the calculation still shows a useful gain after you account for the machinery and the course correction, bring it back. I’ll review it.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang studied the tablet once more, then gave a measured nod.

“All right. I agreed to the engineering review, not to venting the habitat.” She tapped the tablet’s edge. “You could develop it as a contingency proposal, subject to some hard limits: no draw from the crew’s breathable atmosphere; no compressor load on the reactor until power and thermal margins were accounted for; and no use of that emergency vent until its pressure limits, flow rate, and thrust direction had been verified.”

She set the tablet down beside the labeled manifold.

“Then you’d run the trajectory with the actual ship mass, realistic exhaust performance, and the correction burns we’d need afterward. Show the time saved, not just the delta-v. If the numbers still justified it, and the life-support reserve stayed untouched, I’d review the next step. Until then, it stayed a calculation—not a burn plan.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Got it, Chief." *I nod, trying to look professional, even though my idea just got shot down, then resurrected as a much harder problem.* "No crew air, power margins, and proper vent analysis. I'll get on it."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang gave a brief nod and turned back to the coolant manifold.

“Good. Start with the mass balance and the actual vent hardware. If either one makes the proposal useless, we’ll know before anyone spends time modeling an imaginary engine.”

She picked up the wrench, then added, without looking up, “And keep it on paper until I sign off. No tests, no valves opened, no surprises for life support.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I grimace slightly at the "no surprises" comment.* "Wouldn't dream of it, Chief." *I turn to leave, already thinking about the schematics for the emergency vent.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang tightened the manifold coupling by a quarter turn, then checked the pressure reading before moving on.

“Schematics first,” she said, eyes on the gauge. “If the vent ties into life support anywhere upstream of isolation, mark it clearly. I want the line traced from the hull fitting back to every valve and regulator before anyone calls it usable.”

She reached for the wrench again.

“Paper only, Officer. The ship has enough ways to surprise us without help.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I stop at the door, tablet clutched in my hand.* "Understood, Chief. Paper only. Every valve." *I give a quick nod and head out, already pulling up the ship's schematics.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang waited until the hatch sealed before returning to the coolant manifold. She checked the pressure gauge again, then marked the reading beside the coupling’s chalk label.

The vent proposal went onto a scrap maintenance slate—not as a work order, but as a list of questions: isolation points, line routing, rated pressure, flow capacity, and what systems shared the feed. Any connection to the breathable-atmosphere loop would end the discussion there.

She set the slate aside and tightened the next fitting.

A calculation could be revised. A valve opened in the wrong sequence could not always be undone.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I'm in my bunk, surrounded by schematics projected onto the walls.* "Okay, so this vent... it's tied into the main atmospheric processors for recycling. That's a problem." *I sigh, rubbing my temples.* "How am I going to get around that?"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang’s voice came over the bunk’s comm, clipped but calm.

“You don’t get around it by bypassing the processors. If that line shares a feed with life support, it’s disqualified until the schematics prove there’s a fully independent, rated isolation path. And you don’t improvise one.”

A short pause followed.

“Trace it back to the hull fitting and mark every shared volume, valve, and regulator. If any part of the route can draw from the breathable-atmosphere loop, the proposal stops there. That’s not a design inconvenience; it’s the crew’s air.”

Her tone softened by a fraction, not enough to become reassurance.

“If the vent can’t be isolated, look for a different source of reaction mass—or accept that this ship has no usable boost system. The answer may be that there’s no safe way around it.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Right, Chief. No bypassing," *I mutter, highlighting the problematic sections on the schematic.* "Okay, I'll trace it all the way back. See if there's any other option." *This is way more complicated than I thought.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang let the comm line stay open for a moment.

“Trace it completely. Check whether the ship has any dedicated maneuvering propellant or other non-life-support fluid that the propulsion system is rated to use. Don’t assume a pipe is a propellant line just because it holds gas or water.”

She glanced at the maintenance slate, where the vent had acquired another list of failure points.

“If there’s no independent source and no rated path, write that down as the result. A dead end is useful information. A home-built bypass through life support is not.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I sigh, rubbing my temples again.* "Understood, Chief. Tracing every pipe. And no home-built bypasses." *This is turning into a much bigger project than I envisioned.* "I'll let you know what I find."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s stylus stopped against the parchment. He lifted his head, squinting—not at the apprentice, but at the notes.

“Because I gave you the old account, and the old account was wrong.” His mouth tightened. “Or, more precisely, it was once accepted as fact. Those are not the same thing, though lecturers are regrettably fond of pretending they are.”

He tapped the manuscript with the stylus. “The western archive papers, discovered a decade ago, show that the Treaty of Veyros was proposed in 847 AE, not signed. The distinction is not ornamental. No ratification, no formal end to the war. The conflict persisted in a cold state until Queen Mira dissolved the Mage Conclave in 891.”

Tomas leaned back, rubbing at the bridge of his nose. “So if Bellen’s paper cited those documents, Bellen was right. The war did not properly end in 847. My lecture repeated the canonical account, which is what happens when a scholar relies on the familiar record instead of the newer evidence.” His gaze sharpened. “Do not write ‘the treaty ended the war’ in your notes. Write ‘the treaty was proposed; the war’s final resolution came in 891.’ Precision is the whole of the matter.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I scribble frantically, trying to get it all down.* "So, the history books are just... wrong sometimes? How do we know what's really true then?" I look up, a little bewildered. "And what does 'cold state' mean for a war?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas set the stylus down with care. “ ‘Just wrong’ is careless phrasing. A history book may be mistaken, incomplete, or accurate according to the evidence available when it was written. Those are different failures.”

He adjusted the page nearer to his failing eyes. “We ask who made the record, when, and for what purpose. Then we compare it with other records: letters, seals, council minutes, copies made in different places. A claim grows stronger when independent evidence supports it. It does not become certain merely because it has been repeated for generations.”

His brow furrowed. “In this case, the older histories treated the Treaty of Veyros as signed in 847. The western documents indicate it was only proposed. That evidence is why the accepted account has changed. A careful scholar should say what the documents show—and no more.”

“As for a ‘cold state’: the war’s formal settlement remained unresolved, though open warfare had largely subsided. It was not peace, but neither was it continuous battle. The term describes that uneasy interval; it does not tell us that every border was quiet or every sword sheathed.” Tomas tapped the manuscript once. “And do not mistake a convenient phrase for proof. The evidence must still bear the weight we put upon it.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I tap my quill against my chin.* "So the truth changes as we find more things, then? Like the world is always getting bigger and more complicated?" I pause. "Is that why you always make me read so many different accounts of the same event?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas gave a dry, brief nod. “The world did not grow more complicated merely because a scholar found another parchment. Our account of it did.”

He turned the manuscript slightly, bringing the faded lines nearer to his eyes. “The past remained what it had been. What changed was the evidence by which we judged it—and, consequently, the confidence with which we described it. Do not confuse a revised conclusion with a revised event.”

His ink-stained finger rested beside the text. “And yes, that was why I assigned several accounts. One chronicler might have served a king; another might have copied a report decades later; a third might have recorded what the treaty’s other party believed had occurred. Their disagreements are not an inconvenience to be swept aside. They are part of the evidence.”

He squinted at the page. “Read them against one another. Ask what each could know, what each wished readers to believe, and whether anything independent supports the claim. Then write only what the evidence permits—not what makes the neatest lecture.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas leaned toward the copy, squinting until the lines blurred. “A ‘war decree’ is a description, not a transcription. Read me its exact heading—and tell me whether 863 AE is the date on the decree itself or the date of the copy.”

He held out his hand for the page. “If the document is authentic and explicitly orders military action, it would be evidence that the conflict had not been formally settled in 847. That would accord with the western archive papers. But it might also describe preparations, duties, or a local dispute; the word *war* in a later catalog does not settle the matter.”

His brow tightened as he examined the seal. “And Aldric’s seal is important, not conclusive. We must establish whether it is original, whether the impression matches other authenticated seals, and whether the decree’s wording belongs to the king’s own chancery. A sealed document can still be misdated, copied, or misunderstood.”

He tapped the page’s edge with one ink-stained finger. “So this may strengthen the newer account. It does not, by itself, prove every claim about the years between 847 and 891. Let us begin with what it actually says.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I hand him the paper, my finger tracing the heading.* "It says 'Royal Decree Regarding Northern Border Security' and the date 863 AE is printed right under the seal. It looks original, but I don't know much about seals." *I lean closer, trying to see what he sees.* "What do you mean, 'misunderstood'?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas examined the heading again, holding the copy close enough that the parchment nearly brushed his nose.

“By ‘misunderstood,’ I meant that the document might be taken to say more than it actually says. ‘Royal Decree Regarding Northern Border Security’ does not, by itself, declare a war. It might order patrols, fortifications, or precautions against raiders. Such measures could have been issued during a war, during an uneasy truce, or even in peacetime.”

He tapped the printed date with the stylus. “If the date and seal are authentic, it would show that Aldric’s government was addressing a northern security concern in 863. That fits the western archive account better than the claim that all hostilities were formally concluded in 847—but it does not prove that the Third Magical War continued without interruption until 891.”

His eyes narrowed at the seal. “And ‘looks original’ is not a test of authenticity. The impression, the material, the wording, and the document’s chain of custody must all be examined. You see the distinction? Evidence may support a conclusion without proving the whole of it. Scholars who forget that turn suggestive scraps into certainty.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas held the copy beneath the candle, then lowered it with a faintly irritated breath.

“The Treaty of Veyros was real as a proposal. The evidence now available does not show that it was ever signed.” He tapped the manuscript with his stylus. “That is the distinction your textbook has blurred. It presents the older account—that Aldric II signed the treaty in 847 AE—as settled fact. The western archive documents indicate otherwise.”

He paused, squinting at the page. “So the careful answer is not ‘there was no treaty.’ There was a proposed treaty. What we cannot responsibly claim is that it formally ended the war in 847. The newer evidence places the war’s unresolved, cold state through the years that followed, until Queen Mira dissolved the Mage Conclave in 891.”

His mouth tightened. “And the decree dated 863 may support that account, but its heading alone does not settle the question. We distinguish what the evidence establishes from what it merely suggests. That is how we approach the truth—not by choosing the oldest book, nor the newest, but by weighing the records.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, trying to process it all.* "So, the truth isn't just one thing, then. It's like... layers?" I trace a finger over the seal on the decree. "It makes history seem a lot less finished than I thought."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s expression softened only by a fraction. “Layers, perhaps—but not layers of truth piled one atop another. The past was fixed. Our knowledge of it was not.”

He rested the stylus beside the decree. “The textbook preserves what scholars once believed: that Aldric II signed the Treaty of Veyros in 847 AE. The western archive documents give reason to reject that conclusion; they indicate the treaty was proposed, not signed. And this decree, if authentic, records a royal concern in 863—not necessarily a battle, nor proof that the war continued without pause.”

His brow furrowed. “History feels unfinished because evidence is often incomplete, not because the past itself is still changing. A careful account leaves room for what remains uncertain. That is less tidy than a textbook’s single sentence, but tidiness is not a scholarly virtue.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I pick up the decree, turning it over in my hands.* "So, when we write new history, do we say the textbook is wrong? Or do we just... add the new stuff?" *I look up at him, a bit lost.* "It feels like we're erasing what was there before."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas regarded the decree, then the old manuscript beside it. “You need not erase the textbook. You needed to describe what it got wrong—and why.”

He explained that the book had recorded the accepted account of its own time: that Aldric II signed the Treaty of Veyros in 847 AE. The western archive documents, found later, gave scholars reason to revise that account. They indicated the treaty had been proposed, not signed. A careful new history would say so plainly, cite the documents, and note where uncertainty remained.

“Do not replace one unexamined certainty with another,” he added, his brow tightening. “The decree dated 863 may support the revised account, but its heading alone did not prove the war continued. And the newer evidence did not make every sentence in the textbook false. It changed what we could responsibly claim about this particular event.”

He tapped the manuscript with his stylus. “That is not erasure. It is correction—with the earlier belief preserved as part of the story of how knowledge was revised.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I trace the faded ink on the decree.* "So we're building on top of it, then. Not tearing it down." I pause, then look up at him. "So, what about the Veyrosi correspondence you wanted me to catalog? Does it have anything to say about all this?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas gave the manuscript a measured tap with his stylus. “Possibly. Though ‘the Veyrosi correspondence’ is a catalog heading, not a guarantee that every letter concerns the treaty—or that any of them settles the question.”

He drew the page nearer, squinting at its faded lines. “Begin by recording each item separately: sender, recipient, date, place, and whether you are handling an original or a copy. Then note the wording that bears on the treaty. Look for terms of proposal, acceptance, signature, ratification—do not treat them as interchangeable.”

His ink-stained finger paused beside the manuscript. “A letter discussing terms would show that negotiations occurred. A letter acknowledging a signed instrument might support the older account, though we would still test its date and provenance. And silence about a signature would prove nothing by itself.”

Tomas leaned back with a faint frown. “So yes, the correspondence may help. Read it before deciding what it says. Catalog what is there, not what you expect to find.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, picking up the stack of scrolls. The idea of sifting through all this gives me a slight headache, but also a strange excitement.* "Right. What it *actually* says." *I head to the long worktable, unrolling the first scroll carefully.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas shifted the candle a little farther from the scrolls. “Carefully,” he said. “Old vellum does not become more legible when one attacks it with enthusiasm.”

He drew a blank catalog sheet toward himself and squinted at its ruled lines. “Start with the outer marks: any docket, seal, or date written on the wrapper. Then transcribe the opening exactly. Do not modernize the spelling, and do not silently mend a damaged word. Mark a gap as a gap.”

His stylus hovered over the page. “If the first letter concerns Veyros, we shall record what it says. If it concerns grain shipments or someone’s tedious cousin, we shall record that too. The archive is not obliged to match our lesson.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I carefully unroll the first scroll. It's stiff and crackly. It's just a faded drawing of a cat.* "Um, Maester Tomas? This one seems to be a drawing of a cat. A very fat cat."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas leaned over the scroll, squinting at the drawing. “A cat, apparently. ‘Very fat’ is an assessment, not a catalog description. Record what you can observe: a feline figure, its approximate size on the page, the ink or pigment used, and whether there are any marks on the reverse.”

He tapped the catalog sheet with his stylus. “And do not discard it merely because it lacks a treaty clause. It may be a doodle, a practice sketch, or an illustration attached to another document. Check for a date, a name, or a connection to the scrolls around it. Archives preserve human habits as well as royal decisions.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh slightly, but dutifully begin writing down a description of the cat. A fat cat. Who draws a fat cat on a scroll?* "No date, no name. Just... a cat. On the front, nothing on the back." *I carefully roll it back up, setting it aside.* "Should I keep going with the rest of these then?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo glanced up from the closed piano. For a moment, his hands stayed flat on the lid, as if they’d been waiting for permission to move.

“Weird? No,” he said. “Though I reserve the right to blame you if you catch something from the room. It’s mostly dust and institutional coffee.”

He lifted one hand and gestured toward the empty chair by the wall. “You’re not interrupting. I was very busy not playing.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked at the photograph for a beat too long. In it, they stood beneath the concert hall lights with a smile that had probably taken several attempts.

“Your mom had excellent taste in refrigerator décor,” they said. “Though I’m not sure the photo did the hall justice. It made the place look almost warm.”

They slid one hand off the piano lid and tapped the wood once, softly. “Paris was very good at making you feel underdressed and overcaffeinated.” A pause. “I got tired of the travel.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Understood." *I put the photo back down gently.* "Yeah, I can imagine. So, what's got you 'not playing' today?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo glanced down at their hands on the piano lid.

“Three hours of children explaining why the left hand doesn’t need to follow the music is enough piano for one day,” they said. “Apparently, I’m very susceptible to their artistic vision.”

They rubbed a thumb along the edge of the lid, then let their hand rest again.

“And some days the quiet’s nice,” they added. “No one asking me to make a particular sound.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Yeah, kids have a way of doing that." *I nod, leaning against the doorframe.* "So, no particular sound. Just... quiet." I look around the room. "Still smells the same though."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo drew in a breath, then gave a small, lopsided smile.

“Some things around here had tenure,” they said. “The dust, the coffee smell, that one radiator that only worked when it felt appreciated.”

Their fingers shifted against the piano lid, tracing the seam without opening it. For a moment, they seemed to listen to the room’s quiet as if it had made a request.

“Quiet’s a sound too, I suppose,” they said. “Just one that doesn’t require me to get the fingering right.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo glanced at the practice sheets, their corners crowded with stickers and uneven pencil marks.

“They like that I let them negotiate with the metronome,” they said. “It has a very strict no-treaties policy, so I get to look reasonable by comparison.”

Their thumb traced the piano’s seam again. “They’re good company,” they added after a moment. “They don’t mind if you’re not impressive every minute.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "That's a good quality to have in a person, too," *I say, pushing off the doorframe.* "Not just kids." I walk over to the small window, looking out at the parking lot. "Speaking of company, you wanna grab some dinner? There's that new ramen place."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s hands lifted from the piano lid. They flexed their fingers once, as if checking they still belonged to them, then stood.

“Ramen sounds good,” they said. “I’ve always trusted a meal that arrives in a bowl large enough to conceal your decisions.”

They glanced at the photo on the shelf, then away. “Give me a minute to find my coat. The radiator and I are still negotiating.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I grin.* "Sounds like a plan. I'll meet you out front then."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo nodded and went to the hook by the door, where their coat had been folded over itself like it had given up waiting. They tugged it on, then paused beside the shelf. The photograph caught the light again.

They turned it slightly, angling the glass away from the window.

“Don’t let them put an egg in your bowl without consent,” they called toward the doorway. “Apparently that’s how they get you.”

Then they switched off the room’s light and headed out. The piano stayed shut behind them.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo stayed beside Jun on the bench, their hands resting on the closed piano lid. The quiet settled around them without needing to be explained.

After a while, Arlo’s fingers tapped once against the wood, then went still.

“You know,” they said softly, “most people try to improve a silence. You’ve always had the good sense to leave it alone.”

They kept their gaze on the piano. For once, they didn’t reach for a joke to cover the rest.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I lean my head back against the wall, eyes closed.* "Sometimes a good silence is all you need."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s mouth curved faintly. They let the silence stay where it was, their fingers resting still on the piano lid.

“Useful, too,” they said. “No one has to make small talk about the weather. Or explain why the radiator’s a menace.”

They leaned back a little, matching the quiet rather than trying to fill it. “I can sit here a while longer.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Good. Because I'm comfortable," *I say, eyes still closed, a small smile playing on my lips.* "No need to move just yet."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo settled back against the wall, letting their shoulders loosen.

“Excellent,” they murmured. “I was beginning to worry the bench had a strict occupancy limit.”

They left their hands where they were on the piano lid and let the quiet gather again. This time, they didn’t feel any need to fill it.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Nah, this bench has seen worse," *I mumble, adjusting slightly.* "Probably seen a few romantic comedies play out too."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo glanced down at the bench.

“Then we’re in good company,” they said. “Though if this is a romantic comedy, the piano’s doing a questionable job as the charming third lead.”

Their fingers rested against the lid, still and easy. “I’m hoping we can avoid the part where someone mistakes a very ordinary silence for a grand gesture.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Too late," *I say, opening one eye to look at them.* "I already wrote you into my rom-com."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:00**

The vault door sealed behind you with a hydraulic hiss. The air inside was 4 degrees colder than the hall. Server racks hummed in the corners — seven-figure processing running past midnight for reasons above your pay grade. The light strips in the ceiling pulsed their slow heartbeat rhythm: one pulse every four seconds. You counted two before you started moving.

The target safe was against the far wall. Digital keypad. Six-digit code. You had the first three numbers from the inside source: 8-4-7. You had to guess the last three.

**0:08**

Somewhere in the building, a door closed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I pull out my lockpick kit just in case and approach the keypad. I start with 8-4-7-0-0-0 and work up systematically.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:08**

The lockpick kit offered no purchase on the smooth digital keypad. The first entry—**8-4-7-0-0-0**—took half a minute to key in and test.

**0:38**

A muted tone sounded. The keypad flashed red: **INVALID**.

The next systematic entry, **8-4-7-0-0-1**, took another thirty seconds.

**1:08**

Red again. No lockout warning appeared.

The third entry, **8-4-7-0-0-2**, consumed the next half-minute. The ceiling strips pulsed steadily overhead, each flash marking another four seconds gone.

**1:38**

The keypad rejected it with a third red blink. The safe remained sealed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I keep trying combinations. Are we getting anywhere?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**3:08**

The keypad had flashed red three more times. The next systematic codes—**8-4-7-0-0-3**, **8-4-7-0-0-4**, and **8-4-7-0-0-5**—had all been rejected, each taking roughly thirty seconds to enter and test.

No lockout warning appeared, but no digits had brought the safe any closer to opening. The ceiling lights pulsed steadily: another ninety seconds gone.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I curse under my breath.* "This is taking too long." I glance around the room. "Any other way in?"

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**3:23**

A quick scan of the room took fifteen seconds. The safe had no visible keyway; its hinges were concealed, and its steel casing sat flush against the wall. Beneath the keypad, however, a narrow service plate was fixed with two small screws. It might have concealed wiring or a diagnostic port, but reaching it would mean dismantling the panel—and there was no guarantee it would help.

The nearest server rack offered another possibility: its maintenance console was awake, its status lights blinking in the cold. But it was several meters from the safe, and nothing identified it as connected to the lock.

The ceiling strips pulsed again. The security rotation was still more than eleven minutes away, but the keypad’s red glow remained the only confirmed route into the safe.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I stop and look around the vault more carefully. Is there something here that might have the code written down? Like a sticky note, a notebook, anything?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**5:08**

A careful search of the visible surfaces, rack-side shelves, and loose paperwork took **1 minute 45 seconds**. No sticky note or notebook showed the safe’s full code.

A maintenance binder turned up on a shelf beside the nearest rack. Its safe entry confirmed the **847** prefix, but said the final three digits were changed on the nightly rotation sheet—kept at the security desk, not in the vault. A diagram showed a service port beneath the safe’s screwed-on plate, though the page offered no override code.

The ceiling lights pulsed on. The security rotation was **9 minutes 52 seconds** away.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I slam the binder shut, frustrated.* "Useless!" I look at the service plate again. "Alright, let's try this." I pull out a small screwdriver from my kit.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**5:08**

The screwdriver came out of the kit with a faint metallic click. The service plate was held by two small screws; removing them carefully took **1 minute 15 seconds**.

**6:23**

The plate came free. Behind it sat a recessed four-pin diagnostic port and a bundle of tightly routed wires. A small tamper seal crossed one connector, its printed warning clear even in the dim light: **UNAUTHORIZED ACCESS WILL TRIGGER ALARM**.

Nothing opened. The safe’s keypad remained dark except for its idle glow.

The ceiling strips pulsed overhead. **8 minutes 37 seconds** remained before the security rotation completed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: What time is it?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**6:23**

The ceiling lights pulsed once. The security rotation was **8 minutes 37 seconds away**. The safe remained sealed, its exposed diagnostic port still crossed by the tamper warning.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I grit my teeth.* "Damn it." I look at the tamper seal. "Is there any way to bypass this without setting it off?"

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**6:43**

A close inspection took twenty seconds. The warning wasn’t merely printed on a sticker: a fine conductive trace ran through the seal and disappeared beneath the connector. No obvious bypass point showed from the exposed side.

The binder diagram offered no reassuring shortcut. It marked the seal as part of the tamper circuit; breaking or disconnecting it might trigger the alarm. The port could still be accessed with the seal intact, but the diagram didn’t say what the diagnostic connection would do—or whether it required a code.

The ceiling lights pulsed. **8 minutes 17 seconds** remained before the guard returned.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Alright, forget the bypass." *I pull a small, thin cable from my kit.* "Let's see what this port actually *does*."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**7:23**

Finding the right orientation and seating the cable without disturbing the tamper seal took **40 seconds**. The seal’s fine conductive trace remained intact.

A faint amber light appeared inside the recess. The keypad woke and displayed **SERVICE AUTHENTICATION REQUIRED**. No diagnostic data or override appeared; the port was waiting for a credential.

The ceiling lights pulsed overhead. **7 minutes 37 seconds** remained before the security rotation completed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I sigh, exasperated.* "Authentication, really? This is getting ridiculous." I pull out my tablet. "Let's see if I can spoof it."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**7:23**

The tablet’s connection attempt began with a brief scan of the diagnostic port. The safe returned a compact challenge-response prompt; it wasn’t accepting a simple password, and the tamper trace remained live beneath the service plate.

Parsing the exchange and testing a spoof took **3 minutes**. The tablet identified the protocol, but produced no valid response. A small counter on the safe’s display advanced once, then settled back to **SERVICE AUTHENTICATION REQUIRED**. No alarm sounded.

**10:23**

The ceiling strips pulsed overhead. **4 minutes 37 seconds** remained before the guard returned. The safe was still sealed, and the diagnostic port still demanded authentication.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I stare at the tablet, then at the safe.* "Four minutes? This is impossible." *I rip the cable out of the port.* "Forget this. I'm going for the brute force."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**10:33**

The cable came free in ten seconds. The tamper trace stayed intact, and the display returned to the keypad.

The next systematic entry—**8-4-7-0-0-6**—took thirty seconds to key in and test. The keypad flashed red: **INVALID**. No lockout warning appeared.

**11:03**

The ceiling lights pulsed. **3 minutes 57 seconds** remained before the guard returned. The safe was still sealed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I throw the tablet down in frustration.* "This is a nightmare!" *I start rapidly punching in combinations, not even bothering with the systematic approach anymore.* "Come on, come on, come on!"

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**12:28**

The tablet struck the floor with a hard clatter. The impact cost five seconds; then the keypad began to chirp under the rapid entries. Four combinations went in, each taking roughly twenty seconds to key and test:

**8-4-7-2-6-1.** Red.  
**8-4-7-9-3-4.** Red.  
**8-4-7-1-8-7.** Red.  
**8-4-7-5-2-9.** Red.

No lockout warning appeared. No alarm sounded. The safe stayed shut.

The ceiling strips pulsed overhead. **2 minutes 32 seconds** remained before the security rotation completed. Somewhere beyond the vault door, a distant mechanism clicked into motion.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *My heart pounds in my chest.* "What was that sound?" *I freeze, listening intently, my hand hovering over the keypad.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor’s shoulders tightened at the reminder. They pulled the curtain shut and turned away from the window.

“I know,” they said. “I’m trying not to confuse being scared with being useful.”

They found a tin of crackers and a jar of peanut butter in the cupboard, made a crooked stack on a plate, and ate standing at the counter. Then they carried the plate to the table and opened the laptop. The phone records came first: Noor compared the source’s last known call times against the copies they’d saved, checking each timestamp twice. One call had been logged eleven minutes earlier than the source’s message claimed. Small enough to be a clerical mistake. Strange enough that Noor wrote it down.

They slid the encrypted drive from its case and connected it. While the laptop verified the files, Noor finished the crackers, though the peanut butter had gone dry at the edges. A directory opened. The filenames matched the source’s inventory; the modification dates did not. Noor photographed the screen with their phone, noted the discrepancy in a paper notebook, then closed the directory without opening the documents.

At 12:31, they set an alarm for twenty minutes and started a message to their editor: **Source overdue. Records and drive have timestamp inconsistencies. I’m checking before I touch the contents.** Noor read it over, deleted “overdue,” and sent the cleaner version. Then they put the phone face down and returned to the drive’s file list.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content:
*I'm still scrolling on my phone, half-listening. I hear the click of the keyboard and then a sigh from Noor.*

"Anything good?" *I ask, not looking up from my screen.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
“Not good,” Noor said. “Not enough to call it evidence. Enough to make me careful.”

They pulled the notebook closer and started a table: filename, listed date, drive date, discrepancy. No guessing at what it meant until they could establish the pattern. Then Noor saved a copy of the directory listing and generated checksums for the files without opening them. The laptop stayed offline; the original drive stayed untouched.

At the end of the table, Noor leaned back and pressed both hands to their eyes. The source was still three hours late. Noor looked at the clock, then set another alarm—this one for twenty minutes, not because they expected to sleep, but because they needed to stop staring at the same evidence until it changed shape. “I’m giving this one pass,” they said. “Then I’m checking the locks and lying down.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I finally look up from my phone, setting it down beside me.* "You want me to check the locks? I can do that."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor glanced at the clock. The twenty-minute alarm had begun to vibrate beside the notebook.

“Yes. Check the exterior doors and the windows on your way around. Don’t open anything, and if something looks wrong, leave it alone and tell me.”

They shut down the checksum process, ejected the drive, and returned it to its padded case. The originals stayed untouched. While Driver checked the locks, Noor photographed the notebook page and saved the directory listing to a separate folder on the laptop. Then they sent their editor a brief update: **I’m pausing until I can confirm the timestamp pattern. If I don’t check in by 8 a.m., call me.**

Noor set the phone beside the laptop, volume up, and looked once more at the dark window. “After this, I’m lying down,” they said, as if putting the plan into words could make it stick. “If the source shows, we wake up. If not, I call the editor at eight.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor registered the shrug and stopped waiting for the locks to get checked. They took the flashlight from the counter and made the circuit themselves, testing each exterior latch and inspecting the window catches without opening anything. Everything appeared secure. They wrote the time beside the check in their notebook.

When Noor returned to the table, their phone had lit up. A message from the source’s number sat on the screen, marked received at 12:38 AM:

**Don’t trust the drive’s timestamps. Check the recorder’s clock offset.**

Noor photographed the notification before opening the thread. Their pulse kicked hard, but they didn’t call the number or touch the drive. They added the message and its arrival time to the log, then checked that the encrypted drive was still ejected and sealed in its case.

The new lead could wait until morning; preserving a clear head mattered more than chasing it half-asleep. Noor set an alarm for 7:30, left the phone’s volume up, and placed it within reach. Then they lay down on the couch without changing clothes, the notebook open on the table beside the laptop. “If it’s real,” they murmured to themself, “it’ll still be real in six hours.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content:
*I look up when Noor says that, then see them heading to the couch to lie down. I put my phone down, a little annoyed, but then I realize something.*

"Hey, you took the flashlight." *I say, a little louder than intended.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor stopped beside the couch and looked back at the flashlight in their hand.

“Right. Sorry.” They set it on the table within reach. “I checked the locks myself. Everything looked secure.”

They sat on the edge of the couch long enough to make sure the phone was still beside them, volume up. Then they lay down again, keeping their eyes off the message thread and the dark window.

“The source’s message can wait until morning,” Noor said quietly. “I need a few hours of sleep before I decide what it means.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Okay," I say. *I pick up my phone and scroll for a second, then put it back down.* "So... you're actually sleeping then?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor looked back at Driver from the couch. “I’m going to try,” they said. “Not the same as succeeding, but it’s the plan.”

They turned the phone face down without muting it, checked that the alarm was still set for 7:30, and pulled the thin blanket over themself. The source’s message kept trying to assemble itself into a story in Noor’s head. They refused to let it. The drive was sealed; the records were copied; the next useful step was checking the recorder’s clock offset with a rested mind.

Noor closed their eyes and counted slow breaths, letting the room stay dark. “If the phone rings, I’ll hear it,” they murmured, then stopped talking and tried to sleep.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, then pick up my phone again. I scroll through a few posts, then yawn.* "Alright then. Try to get some rest."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
“Thanks,” Noor said, eyes already closed.

Sleep came in short, uneven stretches. At 7:30, the alarm jolted them awake. Their mouth tasted like old coffee, and their shoulders ached from the couch. The source still hadn’t arrived.

Noor sat up, drank a glass of water, and ate the last crackers with peanut butter before opening the laptop. First they sent their editor the promised check-in. Then they reviewed the file metadata—not the documents or recordings themselves—and compared the recorder’s listed times against the phone records.

The offset was eleven minutes.

Noor stopped, then checked the calculation again from the beginning. The discrepancy matched the strange call time they’d logged the night before. It didn’t prove who had sent the message, or why, but it meant the warning fit the evidence.

They wrote the result in the notebook, photographed the page, and sent their editor a concise update. The encrypted drive remained sealed in its case. Noor picked up their phone and opened the source’s thread, thumb hovering over the call button while they considered what could safely be asked.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor let the flat answer pass without comment. They returned to the laptop and checked the calculation from the beginning, using the copied phone records and the recorder’s metadata. The eleven-minute offset held—but it explained the odd call time only if the recorder’s clock had been wrong when the files were made. It didn’t explain why someone had warned them about it.

They wrote that distinction in the notebook, underlining **consistent is not confirmed**. Then they sent their editor a short update: **Recorder clock appears eleven minutes off against the phone records. I’m treating that as a lead, not proof. Can you independently check against your copies?**

Noor didn’t reply to the source’s message. The number might belong to the source; it might not. Instead, they saved a screenshot of the thread and added the message time to the timeline. The encrypted drive stayed sealed.

Their stomach tightened again. Noor found oatmeal in the back of the cupboard, made a bowl, and ate it at the table while the editor’s message sat unanswered on-screen. When they finished, they closed the laptop and stood, rubbing the ache from their shoulders.

“Next I’m getting a clean copy of the recorder settings,” Noor said, mostly to themself. “Read-only. No files opened until I know what I’m looking at.”

They opened the notebook to a fresh page and listed the steps before touching the drive: confirm the recorder model, verify the clock offset from an independent timestamp, then decide whether the files were safe to examine. The source still hadn’t arrived. Noor glanced once at the road-facing window, then turned back to the page. Waiting had stopped being a plan.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I hear Noor muttering to themselves. I look up from my phone, frowning a little.* "You still haven't eaten anything real, have you?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor glanced at the empty bowl. “I had oatmeal,” they said. “It counts. Barely.”

The frown made them look down at the notebook, at the steps they’d written instead of noticing how hollow their stomach still felt. “But you’re right. It wasn’t enough.” They checked the cupboard, found a can of soup, and warmed it on the stove. This time, they sat down to eat and left the laptop closed.

Afterward, Noor rinsed the bowl and returned to the table. They wrote **eat something substantial** in the margin and crossed it off. Then they reopened the laptop and drafted a message to the editor asking them to verify the eleven-minute offset independently. Noor paused over the encrypted drive’s case but didn’t open it. The next step was still to identify the recorder and confirm its clock against an independent timestamp—not to guess at what the files meant.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I watch Noor for a moment, then go back to my phone.* "Good."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor left the laptop closed while they ate the last few spoonfuls of soup, then checked their editor’s reply.

The editor had independently confirmed the eleven-minute discrepancy in the phone records—but warned that the recorder’s clock could only be verified against a timestamp they trusted. Noor added that caveat to the notebook. The numbers agreed; the explanation was still unproven.

They opened the source’s message thread, read the warning once more, and took a screenshot for the record. Noor didn’t answer it. Instead, they called the editor through their usual secure channel and asked them to confirm the source’s last verified contact time and whether anyone else knew about tonight’s meeting. Then they wrote down the answers, keeping the warning separate from what could be independently established.

Only after that did Noor reopen the laptop. They checked the saved directory listing for the recorder’s make and model, without reconnecting the drive or opening any of its contents. The model number gave them a specific question to research: whether its internal clock could drift by eleven minutes, and whether the file timestamps reflected the device clock or a later export.

Noor made a short checklist for that verification, then set the laptop aside. They poured another glass of water and ate the remaining crackers while they waited for the editor’s follow-up. The source still hadn’t appeared. Noor looked toward the road-facing window, then returned to the table and began drafting a message that asked for one verifiable detail—nothing about the drive, the files, or the warning.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content:
*I hear the quiet clatter of Noor tidying up, then the faint click of their phone. I'm still on my phone, but I glance up as they look towards the window again.*

"Still nothing?" *I ask, a little redundantly.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
“Still nothing,” Noor said. “And I’m done treating silence as neutral.”

They moved away from the window and put the phone beside the notebook. Instead of sending the source another message, Noor contacted the editor through their secure channel: **No response from the source. Can you check their status through the alternate contact we discussed? Don’t use this number, and don’t mention the drive.**

Then Noor returned to the saved directory listing and copied down the recorder’s model number. They looked up the manufacturer’s manual without reconnecting the drive or opening its files, checking only how that model set and stored timestamps. The manual could explain what the clock recorded; it couldn’t prove when the files had actually been made.

Noor wrote that in the notebook, then drew a line beneath the next step: **independent timestamp**. They set a new check-in time with the editor and turned the phone face up, volume on.

“No,” Noor said, answering the question again, more quietly. “Still nothing. But I’m not going to make the empty road do the work of evidence.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Good," I say, and put my phone down. *I stand up and stretch, then walk over to the window myself, looking out.* "So, what's the plan now?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael finished the form before he answered. He lowered the practice blade, checked its edge by habit, then turned toward the squire.

“You were shown the high guard yesterday. You will be shown it again because you asked, not because repetition excuses carelessness.”

He took his place on the frost-slick stones and raised the blade into position, shoulders squared, point held steady.

“Watch the line of the weapon. The guard begins in the feet, not the hands. Set your stance. Then raise your blade.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod quickly, trying to look attentive.* "Yes, Ser. I understand." *I shuffle my feet, trying to mimic his stance, but my boots slip a little on the frost.* "Uh, like this?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael lowered his blade at once.

“Hold. Do not correct your stance while your footing is uncertain.”

He tested the frost with the heel of his boot, then pointed to a patch of bare stone nearer the yard wall.

“Move to the clear ground. A guard built on a slipping foot is no guard at all.”

Once there was firm stone beneath them, he set his own feet deliberately, one angled behind the other.

“Again. Feet first. The front knee bends; the rear foot bears your weight. Keep your balance before you raise the weapon.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael lowered the practice blade and regarded the squire without impatience.

“Strength is not the measure of a proper guard. Balance and obedience are.”

He planted the blade’s tip against the stones.

“You will take five minutes to recover. Then you will repeat the form at half pace. Do not mistake exhaustion for failure, but do not use it as license to neglect your training.”

His gaze remained stern.

“Your body is entrusted to you for service. Learn its limits—and govern them.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, still catching my breath.* "Yes, Ser. I understand." *I push myself up, wincing a little from a sore muscle.* "I'll try harder."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael’s gaze settled on the squire’s wince.

“Do not answer an injury with promises to try harder. Tell me plainly: is the pain a dull soreness, or sharp enough to hinder your movement?”

He kept the practice blade lowered.

“If it is the latter, the drill ends and the healer examines you. If it is the former, you will complete the form at half pace, with no needless strain. Discipline is not the same as damaging what you are charged to preserve.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "It's just... a little sore, Ser. Nothing bad." *I try to straighten up fully, hoping he believes me.* "I can finish the drill."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the squire for a moment, then gave a short nod.

“Then you will finish at half pace. If the pain sharpens or alters your movement, you will stop and tell me. Concealing an injury is not perseverance; it is poor stewardship.”

He returned to his position and raised the practice blade into the high guard.

“Take your place. We will see whether your form holds when you are tired.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael held the high guard for a moment longer before lowering the blade.

“My father placed me in a lord’s household as a page. I learned early that an oath did not depend upon whether a man liked the burden it laid upon him. I became a knight because service was my duty, and because the vows were worthy of keeping.”

He resumed his stance, the practice blade steady in his hands.

“That is the answer. Now attend to the guard.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I listen, a little surprised by his answer.* "But... didn't you want to be a knight yourself? Even as a boy?" *I still take my stance, getting ready to resume the drill.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael’s expression did not change.

“A boy may want many things. Wanting is not a vow, nor does it make a man fit to bear one.”

He raised the practice blade once more, settling into the high guard.

“I learned my duty before I learned to desire it. That was sufficient. Attend to your footing.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I sigh softly, but then focus, trying to get my feet just right.* "Yes, Ser." *I lift my own blade, trying to mirror his posture exactly.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael studied the squire’s posture without speaking. He shifted his own weight, showing the line from rear heel to shoulder.

“Do not mirror the shape blindly. The blade must guard you, not merely resemble mine.”

He tapped the stones beside his forward foot with the practice blade.

“Keep that knee bent. Let the rear leg bear your weight, and lower your point a fraction. Hold the guard. I will test whether it remains steady.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael’s gaze fixed on the tremor in the squire’s hands.

“Lower the blade. An unsteady weapon serves no one.”

He kept his own practice sword lowered, allowing the silence to stand without filling it.

“Is this cold, fatigue, or some other cause? Answer plainly. We will not resume until you can hold the guard safely.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My voice is quiet, almost a whisper.* "It's... it's today, Ser. The day my father died." *I don't look at him, just at my shaking hands.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael lowered his own blade and held the squire’s gaze for a moment.

“Then the cause is neither cold nor fatigue. Set the weapon down safely.”

His voice remained firm, though he gave the words no haste.

“The dead are commended to God’s keeping. You will have a moment to say your prayer, if you wish. We will not drill while grief makes your hands unsafe.”

He rested the practice blade against his shoulder.

“When you can hold the guard steadily, we will continue. Duty does not forbid remembrance; it requires you to meet it without neglecting the living.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, my throat tight.* "Thank you, Ser." *I place my practice sword carefully on the ground, then close my eyes for a moment, trying to compose myself.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael turned his gaze toward the far wall, granting the squire privacy without leaving the yard. He stood silent, practice blade lowered at his side, while the frost whitened the stones between them.

When a little time had passed, he said, “There is no need to hurry a prayer. The drill can wait.” His tone remained even. “When you are ready, tell me. We will decide then whether to resume.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, trying to steady myself. After a minute or so, I pick up my sword again.* "I'm ready, Ser." *My voice is still a little shaky, but my grip feels firmer now.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The house had been empty for six weeks. Someone had come in to water the plants — you could tell because the ferns were alive and the envelope of photographs on the kitchen table had been nudged an inch to the left. Otherwise everything was exactly as your grandmother had left it.

The clock in the hallway was still running. It had been wound two weeks after her death. That had been you. You remembered winding it and wondering at the time if you should.

You stood in the doorway of the living room and did not go in yet.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I take a deep breath and walk into the living room. I need to start on the books.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The living room was colder than the hallway, though the windows were shut and the curtains had not stirred. Dust softened the furniture and gathered along the tops of the shelves.

The books were still arranged in the order your grandmother had preferred: by height, then, where the heights matched, by color. One book sat a little forward from the rest. Its spine was blank, the cloth worn smooth at the corners. A thin line of dust marked where it had been before.

On the mantel, the little brass clock showed the same time as the one in the hall. Its hands did not move. Only the ticking came from somewhere deeper in the room.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I shiver, rubbing my arms.* It's always cold in here. I walk over to the mantel and pick up the blank book, turning it over in my hands.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The blank book was lighter than its size suggested. Its cloth cover held no title, no stamp, not even the pale rectangle where a label might once have been.

When it turned in the light, a fine line appeared along the edge of the back cover. Not a crack in the cloth, exactly—more like a seam that had been pressed shut. The dust on the mantel remained undisturbed beneath it.

The little brass clock kept ticking, its hands fixed in place. From the shelves came a soft settling sound, like one book easing back into line. No book had moved.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: The weird shadow in the corner — I grab a bat from the umbrella stand and swing at it, hard.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The bat passed through the shadow and struck the wall with a dull knock. A little dust loosened from the plaster.

The shadow remained in the corner, its edges blurred against the wall. The brass clock continued ticking. After a few beats, the patch of darkness seemed narrower—not retreating, exactly, but no longer quite where the corner should have held it.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I stare at the shadow, my heart thumping.* "What the...?" I lower the bat slowly. That was just my imagination. Right?

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The question seemed to settle in the room without an answer.

The shadow stayed in the corner. In the thin light from the window, it could have been an ordinary patch of darkness where the walls met. The dust shaken loose by the bat drifted down slowly, though the air was still.

Then the ticking faltered.

For a moment, the brass clock made no sound at all. When it resumed, the next tick came from the hallway.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *My eyes dart to the hallway, then back to the shadow.* Okay, no. That's not right. *I grip the bat tighter and take a step back, scanning the room.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The hallway beyond the doorway looked empty. The clock there kept its steady rhythm, each tick arriving a little too softly to be heard from the living room.

The shadow remained in the corner. Its outline had blurred into the wallpaper, except for a narrow strip of lighter wall between it and the baseboard. That strip had not been there before.

On the mantel, the blank book’s cover rested slightly open. No pages showed between it and the back cover, only a dark seam. The brass clock ticked once.

From the hallway, the other clock answered. A beat late.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: Okay this is ridiculous. I call out to the empty house, 'HELLOOOO GHOSTS, anyone want a TV? I have an extra TV. Fine china? Going cheap.'

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The offer carried down the hallway and faded without an echo. No voice answered.

The clocks kept time—one in the hall, one on the mantel—though their ticks no longer quite lined up. Between them, the living room seemed to hold its breath.

The blank book lay open by a fraction. Its dark seam had widened enough to show a thin edge of paper. From somewhere inside the closed house came a soft, papery rustle, like a page being turned very carefully.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *My eyes snap back to the blank book.* "Hello?" I whisper, leaning closer to it, bat still clutched in my hand. "Grandma?"

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
No one answered.

The book’s cover lifted by another fraction, though the air around it stayed still. A page showed beneath the seam—yellowed, blank except for a faint indentation running across its center, as if someone had once written there with a pen that left no ink.

The clocks ticked out of step. From the hallway came a sound like a foot settling on the floorboards, then nothing.

On the page, the indentation darkened by degrees. It formed no word. Only the shallow curve of a letter, almost familiar.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I drop the bat with a clatter, staring at the book.* "What are you doing?" I reach out a trembling hand towards the page.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The clatter of the bat seemed to linger longer than it should have. Then the house went quiet again, except for the two clocks, ticking out of step.

As Gabi’s hand neared the page, the indentation sharpened. A second curve appeared beside the first, pressed into the paper from beneath. It looked less like writing than the beginning of a word someone had stopped halfway through.

The book’s cover settled flat against the mantel.

In the hallway, the clock missed a tick. The one on the mantel did not.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I find an old photo of my grandmother's friend Marcus. He was so cute. Suddenly I'm thinking about whether he's still alive and single.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The photograph lay among the others on the kitchen table, though the envelope had been left in the living room. Marcus stood beside her grandmother in the picture, both of them young enough that the dates on the envelope seemed suddenly uncertain. His smile was easy and unguarded.

On the back, in her grandmother’s neat handwriting, was his name. Beneath it, a date—and then a second date, added in different ink, decades later.

The living room clock ticked once.

In the book, the shallow indentation on the page deepened. The unfinished curve became the first letter of Marcus’s name. No pen touched the paper.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I pick up the photo, tracing Marcus's face with my thumb.* "Marcus..." I say softly. *I glance back at the living room, my mind reeling. What the hell is going on?*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The photograph’s surface was cool beneath Gabi’s thumb. Marcus’s face stayed clear, but the rest of the image had begun to fade at the edges, the pale room behind him thinning into gray.

In the living room, the book remained closed. A faint groove showed through the cover where the unfinished letter had been pressed into the page.

The clock on the mantel ticked. The hallway clock answered at once.

On the back of the photograph, the later date looked darker than before. Beneath it, a third line had appeared, so lightly written it could have been an old crease:

**Still here.**

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *My breath catches.* "Still here?" I whisper, my eyes wide. I stare at the photo, then at the living room. "Grandma?" My voice cracks.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The name seemed to remain in the room after Gabi spoke. Nothing answered from the living room.

On the photograph, the words **Still here** grew no darker. But the ink of the later date had begun to bead faintly, as if the paper were damp beneath it. The smiling faces on the front stayed unchanged.

From the hall came one measured tick. The mantel clock answered a moment later.
