Then, from the living room, the book’s cover lifted and settled once. The sound was small—no louder than a page released between two fingers.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *My heart is pounding.* I take a shaky breath and walk back towards the living room, still clutching the photo. "Grandma, are you... are you really here?"

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The office was the same as always. The same ficus in the corner that was slowly dying despite Dr. Vasquez's best efforts. The same two chairs angled toward each other, not quite facing. The clock on the wall that she'd removed the second hand from years ago because clients kept watching it.

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let five full seconds pass without filling the silence.

“ You found their journal,” she said quietly. “What happened when you opened it?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shrug, still not looking at her.* "I didn't open it. Not yet."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let five full seconds pass.

“You hadn’t opened it yet,” she said. “What made you stop there?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I stop talking mid-sentence. I can't finish it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let five full seconds pass.

“You stopped mid-sentence,” she said quietly. “Would it help to stay with the words you couldn’t finish, or with what it was like to find the journal?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath.* "What it was like to find it. I guess."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let five full seconds pass.

“You wanted to stay with what it was like to find it, not what might be inside,” she said quietly. “What was the first thing you noticed when you realized what it was?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let five full seconds pass.

“You said they wrote about you in the last entry,” she said quietly. “What was it like to know that, without telling me what the entry said?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head, looking down at my hands again.* "I don't know what to do with it."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let five full seconds pass.

“You didn’t know what to do with the fact that they wrote about you,” she said quietly. “When you say ‘do with it,’ what feels like it needs to happen next?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I pick at a loose thread on my jeans.* "I don't know if I should read it or burn it."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let five full seconds pass.

“You were weighing reading it against burning it,” she said quietly. “What did each choice seem to mean to you?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I finally look up at her.* "Reading it means... it's real. Burning it means... it's over."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let five full seconds pass.

“Reading it meant it was real. Burning it meant it was over,” she said quietly. “What did you imagine would be real—or over—if you chose either one?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "If I read it... I have to face it. All of it." *My voice cracks a little.* "Burning it... maybe I could forget."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let five full seconds pass.

“You said reading it would mean facing all of it, and burning it might let you forget,” she said quietly. “What would forgetting give you a break from?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I laugh, a short, bitter sound.* "Everything. Just... everything."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let five full seconds pass.

“Everything,” she said quietly. “What felt like the part you most wanted a break from right then?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "The constant... ache." *I hug myself, almost rocking slightly.* "It just never stops."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let five full seconds pass.

“You called it a constant ache, one that never stopped,” she said quietly. “When did you notice it most today?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "When I found the journal." *My voice is barely a whisper.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The first arrow hit the rocks three feet from Kira's head.

"Contact!" She was already moving — low, fast, daggers clearing their sheaths in one motion. The ravine walls climbed thirty feet on either side. Perfect killzone. The ambushers had the high ground and they knew it.

Another arrow. This one close enough to hear it split the air.

"Cap, I count six on the east ridge, maybe more on the west. We're boxed." She pressed her back against a boulder. Eyes up. Breathing controlled. Waiting for orders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Kira, east ridge — draw their fire. I'll push west with the vanguard."

I raise my polearm and signal the advance.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira gave one sharp nod and broke from the boulder.

She sprinted along the ravine floor, cutting for a narrow patch of open ground where the ridge had a clean shot. An arrow cracked against the stone beside her; another skimmed past her shoulder. She kept moving, then darted behind a jutting slab and flashed one dagger toward the east ridge.

“Come on, then, you bastards!”

A bowstring snapped above. Kira shifted cover before the arrow struck, then peered around the rock long enough to mark two archers loosing from the same outcrop. “Two together, high shelf!” she called, and moved again, keeping their eyes—and their fire—on her.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
*I nod, satisfied Kira's got their attention.* "Alright, vanguard, with me! Push up the west!"

*I charge forward, polearm leading, looking for cover.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The west ridge erupted with movement as the vanguard pushed in. Kira saw several archers turn toward the charge, their bows swinging off her.

“About damn time,” she muttered.

She broke from the slab and sprinted for the base of the east slope, staying tight to the ravine wall. An arrow struck behind her. Another clattered off stone ahead. She dropped behind a low shelf, then spotted one archer fumbling to nock another shaft while his companions tracked the west.

Kira flicked a dagger toward the shelf—not to hit, but to make him flinch—then surged for the narrow, broken path climbing toward the outcrop.

“East ridge is thinning!” she shouted. “I’m moving up!”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: An archer targets me directly. I see the draw.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira caught the bowman turning his aim toward the Captain. “Bowman on the west!” she shouted.

She planted a boot on the broken slope and snapped her remaining dagger toward the archer’s bow hand, then kept climbing, reaching for the ridge before the others could draw another clean shot. “Keep their heads down!”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I grunt, deflecting the arrow with my polearm shaft.* "Got it, Kira!" *I signal two of the vanguard to lay down suppressing fire on that archer.* "Keep pushing!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The answering volley hammered the west ridge, forcing the bowman to duck behind the rocks.

Kira used the noise to close the last few yards. She hauled herself over the lip of the east shelf and landed low, one dagger ready. The two archers she’d marked were still there—one crouched to reload, the other twisting toward the sudden pressure from below.

She lunged at the reloading archer, slashing across his bow arm before he could bring the weapon up. The second archer stumbled back, fumbling for a knife.

“East shelf is mine!” Kira called, stepping between them and the ravine. “One’s down. One’s got steel!”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I'm separated from the group. Kira can see me across the ravine but can't reach me.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira’s gaze snapped across the ravine. The Captain was cut off from the vanguard, with open ground between them and the west ridge still above him.

“Cap! You’re isolated—west ridge has the high ground!” she shouted.

The knife-wielding archer lunged. Kira turned into the attack, caught his wrist with her forearm, and drove her dagger toward his ribs. She shoved him back toward the rocks, keeping herself between him and the ravine’s edge.

“Can’t reach you from here,” she called, eyes flicking back across the gap. “I’ll clear this shelf and look for a crossing!”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Negative, Kira. Hold your position." *I plant my polearm, using it to vault onto a small ledge, looking for a path up.* "I'll clear this side."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
“Copy. Holding.”

Kira kept her ground on the east shelf, turning the knife-wielder’s stumble into an opening. She knocked his wrist aside and drove a boot into his chest, sending him sprawling against the rocks. Her dagger stayed trained on him as she checked the wounded archer nearby.

Movement on the west ridge caught her eye. A bowman was shifting between rocks, trying to find a clear angle across the ravine.

“West ridge, above your ledge!” she shouted. “One bowman moving for a shot. I’m pinned here, but I’ve got this shelf contained.”

She stayed low, using the outcrop for cover, and watched both the fallen archer and the ridge.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I curse under my breath as I see the bowman.* "Dammit." *I duck behind the ledge, my polearm raised to deflect any incoming arrows.* "Vanguard, suppress that archer!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard the vanguard’s volley crack across the ravine. The west-ridge bowman ducked behind the rocks, his shot spoiled.

“Good. Keep him there,” she called.

The knife-wielder was already scrambling for his weapon. Kira stepped in and kicked it out of reach, then pinned his arm beneath her boot. Her eyes stayed on the ridge as she kept her dagger trained on him.

“East shelf is still contained,” she shouted. “But I can’t hold it and watch your flank forever.”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "I'm almost there!" *I scramble up the last few feet of the ledge, pulling myself onto the west ridge.* "Clear the shelf and link up with the vanguard!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
“Copy!”

Kira wrenched the pinned archer’s arm behind his back and struck the back of his head with her dagger pommel. He went limp beneath her boot.

The wounded bowman tried to crawl for his weapon. Kira kicked it farther down the shelf, then slashed his bowstring and shoved him against the rock.

“East shelf clear,” she called across the ravine. “Moving to the vanguard.”

She checked the broken path ahead, then started down the far side of the outcrop, keeping low beneath the ridge line and both daggers ready.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I nod, relieved.* "Good work, Kira! Fan out, see if there are any more of these bastards lurking about."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira followed the broken path down from the shelf, daggers held low and ready. She kept to the rocks, scanning the ridge line and the ravine floor for movement.

“Copy. I’ll check the eastern approach,” she called, then slowed at a bend where the path narrowed. A snapped branch lay across the stones, too fresh to have been there long.

She crouched and listened. Somewhere beyond the rocks, loose gravel shifted.

“Could be another one,” she muttered, easing forward with one dagger angled toward the sound. “I’m checking it out.”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Hold on, Kira. Don't engage alone." *I quickly scan the west ridge, making sure it's secure.* "I'm coming with you."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira stopped at the bend and sank lower behind the rocks, keeping her dagger angled toward the gravelly slope.

“Copy. I’m holding,” she called back, quiet now. She shifted just enough to keep the narrow path in view without exposing herself. “Fresh tracks, maybe. Whatever’s out there hasn’t shown itself yet.”

She listened, still as stone, and waited for the Captain to close the distance.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I move quickly to Kira's position, my polearm held ready.* "Alright, what do we have?" *I peer around the bend, trying to spot any movement.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira kept low and pointed to the snapped branch and a line of fresh scuffs in the dirt.

“Someone came through here recently. One set of tracks, maybe two.” She listened, eyes fixed on the bend. A faint scrape came from beyond it—then a scatter of pebbles clicked down the slope.

Her grip tightened around her daggers. “There. Just past the turn. Could be trying to circle behind us.”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Quiet." *I hold up a hand, listening intently.* "Sounds like one, maybe two. Let's box them in."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable slid the poetry volume into place, then adjusted it by half an inch.

“New is a flexible term,” they said. “Some of it’s merely new to the shelves. Some of it’s been in the back long enough to qualify as a tenant.”

They glanced toward the narrow aisle leading to the storeroom. “Anything you’re looking for, or shall I let the piles make their case?”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Just... anything good." I shrug, running a hand through my damp hair. "It's my last day here, you know?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s hand paused on the nearest stack of books. They straightened it, though it was already straight.

“I know,” they said. “I was hoping you’d ask for something more difficult than ‘anything good.’ It would have given me an excuse to rummage.”

They turned toward the narrow aisle to the back, then stopped to nudge a book into line on the counter. “There’s a slim collection of essays back there. Rather good, and thoroughly unhelpful about endings. Most books are.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable turned the abandoned volume until its spine sat square with the edge of the counter.

“You don’t need to finish the sentence on my account,” they said. “I’ve endured worse openings. Dickens, for instance.”

They let their hand rest on the book a moment longer than necessary, then stepped back. “Take your time.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "No, it's not that." I sigh, looking out the window at the rain. "It's just... I'm gonna miss this place. And you."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable looked down at the abandoned volume and squared it with the counter. Then they shifted it a fraction the other way.

“That was an inconveniently decent thing to say,” they murmured.

They kept their eyes on the book for another moment. “I’ll miss you too. The shop will pretend it’s entirely about having fewer people to complain about the rain to.” A pause. “It won’t be convincing.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach across the counter and put my hand on the book Sable is holding. Our hands are almost touching.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s fingers went still beneath the edge of the book. For once, they didn’t adjust it.

“The books are usually better at holding a conversation,” they said, though the dry remark came out softer than intended.

They drew a careful breath and looked at the narrow space between their hands. “I suppose I could find you something to take with you. A book, I mean. Something suitably unhelpful about leaving.” A pause. “Unless you’d rather I just let that stand.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I'd rather you didn't let it stand." I meet their eyes, a small smile playing on my lips. My hand stays where it is.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable held their gaze for a beat, then let out a quiet breath.

“Then I won’t,” they said.

Their fingers stayed beneath the book, still and close to Wren’s hand. Sable didn’t move nearer. “I’m not particularly good at farewells. I can offer you an essay collection and several opinions about its author, but I gather that’s not what you meant.” A faint, wry smile touched their mouth. “So I’ll try the less literary version: I don’t want this to be the last time I see you.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Good." I intertwine my fingers with theirs. "I don't want it to be the last time either."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s fingers closed around Wren’s, careful but unmistakable. For once, they left the book crooked on the counter.

“Good,” they said, and the word came out without its usual coat of irony.

Their gaze dropped briefly to their joined hands. “Then we’ll have to arrange something less terminal than a farewell. Coffee, perhaps. Or a visit to a bookshop with marginally fewer structural hazards.”

A pause. Sable’s thumb rested against Wren’s knuckles, still as a bookmark. “I’d like that.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I'd like that very much." I squeeze their hand gently. "How about... this weekend? I'll be settled in by then."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s thumb shifted once against Wren’s knuckles.

“This weekend,” they said. “A remarkably sensible proposal. I’ll try not to let it alarm me.”

They glanced at the book still crooked on the counter, then left it there. “Coffee sounds good. Tell me where you’ll be settled, and I’ll find a place nearby—preferably one where the chairs don’t appear to have been condemned by a committee.” A pause, their expression softening despite themself. “I’m looking forward to it.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Okay, it's [New City Name] then." I smile, a genuine, warm smile this time. "I'll text you the details once I'm there."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable gave the city’s name a small, thoughtful nod, as though filing it somewhere more reliable than memory.

“Then I’ll wait for the details,” they said. “Try not to settle somewhere with a café that serves coffee as an act of hostility.”

Their hand remained around Wren’s, easy and careful. The crooked book stayed crooked.

“And when you text,” Sable added, a faint smile at the corner of their mouth, “I’ll have a shortlist ready. I’m told this is what people do when they’re looking forward to seeing someone.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "You're a dork, you know that?" I tease, squeezing their hand one last time before letting go. "I'll text you." I give them a quick wave and head out, feeling lighter than I have in weeks.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell gave its small, bright complaint as the door closed.

Sable looked at the crooked book on the counter. They left it that way for several seconds, which was practically a public declaration.

“Dork,” they murmured to the empty shop. “A term of such precision.”

Then they picked up the book and slid it back into place—carefully, this time, without trying to make the moment fit between its covers. Their shortlist could wait until after closing. Or until tomorrow. There was no need to appear eager.

Sable began straightening the poetry section again. It didn’t need it. Neither did they.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
*I'm walking down the street, still smiling. I pull out my phone and open a new message, typing quickly.*

"He called me sensible! Can you believe it?"

*I hit send, knowing my best friend will appreciate the update.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable made it through eleven minutes before abandoning the poetry section.

They went to the desk, pulled a scrap of paper from beneath a ledger, and began a list of cafés in [New City Name]. The first was crossed out for its chairs. The second for its coffee. The third survived, though Sable added a question mark beside it.

This was not eagerness. It was due diligence, a practice antiquarians applied to objects of uncertain provenance.

They set the list beneath the ledger and returned to the counter. The crooked book had been put away properly now. Sable considered taking it back out, then thought better of making a habit of symbolism.

The bell stayed quiet. The rain kept at the windows.

Sable resumed alphabetizing the poetry section, still not needing to.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
*My phone buzzes a few minutes later with a reply.*

"No way! He's totally into you. You're going to have to tell me EVERYTHING."

*I grin, already thinking about all the details I'll share later.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the alarm before you see the lights. Red, pulsing, flooding the corridor in waves. The defector — Mira, she tells you her name is Mira — leans heavier on your shoulder. Her left leg isn't working right. You don't look at it.

The stairwell door ahead is still clear. For now. You count floors in your head: four to the garage, three to the service tunnel, two to certain capture. The radio in your ear gives you static. Your handler has gone silent.

"How many?" Mira asks. Her voice is steady. Steadier than yours would be.

You don't answer. You move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I check the stairwell. Listen for footsteps below before committing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Below the stairwell door, footsteps climb in measured pairs—two people, moving fast but not running. They stop one landing down.

A radio crackles through the gap. “Upper floors first. Check every door.”

Mira’s grip tightens on your shoulder. The red alarm light pulses across the door’s narrow window. No footsteps come from above. Not yet.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Damn it." *I glance at Mira, then back at the door.* "They're coming up. We can't go down."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira’s eyes flick to the ceiling, then to the corridor behind you. “Then we go up,” she whispers. “There’s a maintenance bridge on the next floor. It connects to the east block.”

Below, the stairwell door handle turns a fraction. The footsteps start again—closer now, measured and quick. A beam of white light sweeps across the narrow window, cutting through the pulsing red.

From above, somewhere beyond the corridor bend, a door slams. Then silence.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I hear them coming from below. I reverse direction — up, not down. I pull Mira with me.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The stairwell rises into darkness, each landing washed red by the alarm lights. Below, the search team’s footsteps accelerate—then stop at the door you just left.

Mira keeps close, favoring her left leg. Above, a door latch clicks.

A thin bar of white light cuts across the next landing as the door opens from the other side. Someone steps into the stairwell. You hear the faint scrape of a weapon being raised.

Mira’s breath catches. “That’s not our way out,” she whispers.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I push Mira back, shielding her.* "Stay behind me." I draw my sidearm, aiming at the sliver of light. "Who's there?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The figure beyond the door freezes. The weapon’s silhouette stays trained through the narrow opening.

“Security,” a voice answers—too calm, too close. “Put the gun down and step away from her.”

Mira goes rigid behind you. Her fingers clutch your sleeve, then loosen as if she’s forcing herself not to pull you back.

Below, the search team reaches the landing. A radio crackles: “Contact on the upper stairwell.”

The door above begins to swing wider. In the gap, you catch a glimpse of a dark sleeve—and a glint of metal.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I set Mira down in the server room and barricade the door. I need to think.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The server-room door shudders against the barricade. A flashlight beam slices beneath it, then disappears.

Mira lowers herself beside a rack of humming servers, jaw clenched against the pain in her leg. The alarm paints her face red, then black, then red again.

Outside, a voice cuts through the door. “Check this room.”

A second voice answers from farther down the hall. “Stairwell’s clear. They must be inside.”

Mira looks toward the rear wall, where a maintenance diagram is bolted between the server racks. “There’s a cable chase behind that panel,” she whispers. “It leads to the east block.”

The barricade scrapes against the floor. Someone tests the handle again—harder this time.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I look at the panel, then the door.* "No time. Not yet." I check my sidearm. "Stay low."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The barricade jumps under a heavy blow. A server rack shivers, its fans whining louder as the door takes another hit.

Mira stays low beside the maintenance diagram. “The panel opens inward,” she whispers. “If they see it move, they’ll know where we went.”

A flashlight beam slips under the door and crawls across the floor, stopping just short of her boot. Then the light vanishes.

“On three,” someone says outside.

Mira’s gaze shifts from the door to the cable-chase panel. Her hand hovers near its edge. The barricade groans as the first impact lands.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I shove the barricade harder against the door.* "Wait for it." My eyes are on the panel, then the door. "Can you open it quietly?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira gives a tight shake of her head. “Not quietly. The latch sticks.”

The first blow lands. The barricade bucks against the door, and the flashlight beam returns beneath it, sweeping toward the server racks.

Mira reaches for the panel anyway, fingers poised at its seam. “I can hold it until the door breaks,” she whispers. “Then we move.”

Outside, boots shift into position.

“Two.”

The panel’s edge catches the pulsing red light. The door groans inward against the barricade.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "No!" *I grab her arm, pulling her away from the panel.* "You distract them, I'll go for the panel."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira stumbles back from the panel, catching herself against a server rack. Her eyes snap to yours, alarm and pain tightening her expression.

The door slams inward. The barricade skids several inches, its legs shrieking across the floor.

“Three!” someone shouts outside.

Mira’s hand closes around a loose metal bracket on the floor. She glances at the door, then at the panel. “I can draw them off,” she whispers. “But you need seconds.”

The next impact rattles the latch. A thin crack opens between the door and its frame, and a flashlight beam knifes through.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Do it!" *I push her towards the door, then crouch by the panel, fumbling for the latch.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira catches the loose bracket and hurls it against the far end of the room. The clang rings over the server fans.

“Here!” she shouts, limping toward the opposite racks.

The flashlight beam jerks away from the crack in the door. Boots pound across the hall, then stop as someone slams against the room’s other side. The barricade shifts—but the pressure on the door eases.

At the panel, the latch sticks beneath your fingers. Metal grates softly against metal.

Behind you, Mira sucks in a sharp breath. “They’re through!”

The door bursts inward. The barricade crashes against the floor, and white light floods the room. A shadow fills the entrance as a weapon rises. The panel gives a sudden, sharp click.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I pull the panel open just as a guard bursts in. No time to secure it.* "Get in!" I grab Mira and shove her through the opening.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira tumbles through the opening and lands hard in the cable chase, biting back a cry. The passage is barely wide enough to crawl through, crowded with conduit and dust.

The guard fills the doorway. His weapon snaps toward the open panel.

A shot cracks through the server room. Sparks spit from the panel’s edge, and the sound ricochets through the narrow passage. Mira scrambles deeper into the darkness, dragging her injured leg behind her.

“Move!” she hisses from ahead. “It drops into the east block!”

The guard steps over the fallen barricade. His flashlight pins the opening in a white glare.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I return fire, hoping to suppress him, then dive headfirst into the crawl space.* "Coming!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your shots hammer the server room. The guard ducks behind the doorframe, and his answering burst chews sparks from the cable-chase entrance.

The passage swallows the alarm’s red glow. Dust shakes loose from the ceiling as rounds strike the wall behind you. Ahead, Mira crawls fast despite her bad leg, one hand dragging along the conduit for balance.

“Drop’s just ahead,” she calls back. “Watch the—”

The floor falls away beneath her words. A metal rung rattles somewhere below, followed by a hollow clang. Mira freezes at the edge of the descent. Behind you, the guard’s boots scrape closer to the panel.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Watch the drop, I got it!" *I squeeze past her, dropping into the gap. It's a long way down.* "You next!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You entered the throne room exactly when the Herald announced you — not a second before, not a second after. Protocol mattered here. Every pair of eyes in the room tracked your approach down the marble aisle.

Queen Isara sat the throne like she'd been carved there. To her right, Commander Ash stood at parade rest with his hand resting on his sword pommel — a statement, not a threat. Officially. Priestess Yuna occupied the observer's alcove, her expression as blank as the icons behind her. Lord Daven caught your eye from the gallery and gave the smallest possible nod.

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. "The court recognizes the Ambassador of Velheim. You may approach and state your purpose."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content:
I bow — exactly the depth required by protocol, no deeper. I address the Queen directly.

"Your Majesty. I bring terms from Velheim regarding the northern trade routes. I request the court's attention and patience."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Queen’s gaze remained fixed on you, cool and assessing. “The court will hear the terms. Whether it will grant them patience remains to be seen.”

The Herald struck the floor once with his staff. “Her Majesty permits the Ambassador of Velheim to present the proposal.”

Commander Ash’s fingers stayed near his sword pommel. “Northern routes are not merely lines on a map. Velheim’s ships have tested our patrols before.”

“Accusation is not evidence, Commander,” Lord Daven said from the gallery, his voice smooth but edged. “Let the terms be heard before the court condemns them.”

Priestess Yuna watched in silence for a moment, then spoke with measured calm. “Trade carries more than goods. The court should learn what else Velheim intends to send along those roads.”

Queen Isara lifted one hand, and the room fell still. “Proceed, Ambassador. Be precise.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet the Queen's gaze, a small, knowing smile playing on my lips.* "Indeed, Your Majesty. Precision is Velheim's strength." *I glance at Commander Ash, then Priestess Yuna.* "My kingdom wishes to discuss a mutual protection pact for all vessels, regardless of origin, within the disputed waters."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
For a moment, the court held its silence around your proposal. The Queen’s expression did not change, but her attention sharpened.

“A mutual pact,” Queen Isara said. “An elegant phrase. It leaves unanswered who would command the patrols, who would judge a breach, and whose waters these ‘disputed’ waters are.”

Commander Ash’s jaw tightened. “Velheim asks our ships to protect its vessels in waters its captains have already tested. That is not mutual protection. It is a demand for our restraint.”

Lord Daven rose from the gallery. “Or an opportunity to establish rules before the next incident gives either side cause to mobilize. A pact could protect the crown’s trade as readily as Velheim’s.”

Priestess Yuna’s gaze moved from the Queen to the Commander. “Then the terms must name the limits as clearly as the protections. Otherwise, the pact will shelter whoever is most willing to exploit its silence.”

The Herald struck the floor once. “The court has heard the initial objections.”

Queen Isara leaned back against the throne. “The court will hear the details next. Ambassador, what protections did Velheim offer in return—and what authority did Velheim expect this court to surrender?”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: I address Commander Ash directly, ignoring protocol. "Commander. Your ships have been blockading our merchants for six weeks. Would you like to explain that to the court, or shall I?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The direct accusation cut through the chamber’s formal quiet. Commander Ash’s hand tightened on his sword pommel, but he did not draw. His eyes stayed on you.

“Those ships were stopped under a royal order,” Ash said. “Velheim’s merchants entered waters under dispute and refused inspection. The blockade prevented further passage until their captains answered for it.”

Lord Daven rose fully from the gallery. “A royal order is not an explanation, Commander. On whose authority were the inspections imposed—and why was the court not told they had continued for six weeks?”

The Herald lifted his staff, then paused as Queen Isara raised one finger. The court fell silent again.

“Commander Ash will answer the question,” the Queen said. Her voice remained cool, though her gaze had shifted briefly to the commander. “And the Ambassador will remember that this court—not its officers—determines who speaks and when.”

Ash’s jaw set. “The order came through the Admiralty. The inspections continued because Velheim’s captains refused to comply.”

Priestess Yuna’s expression remained unreadable. “Refusal to comply with what terms, Commander? A vessel cannot be judged for breaking a rule no one has stated.”

For the first time, Ash looked toward the Queen before replying. “The inspection protocols were issued to the patrol fleet.”

Queen Isara’s gaze sharpened. “Then the court will see them. Until then, the blockade’s justification remains an assertion, not a finding.”

The Herald struck the floor once. “The court requests the Admiralty’s written orders and the records of the stopped vessels.”

The Queen returned her attention to you. “The matter has become relevant to the proposed pact. Ambassador, the court will hear what authority Velheim seeks—and what limits it is prepared to accept.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I smile thinly.* "Your Majesty, Velheim seeks only what is just. We propose a joint commission to adjudicate all maritime disputes, with representatives from both our kingdoms."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Queen let the proposal rest in the silence before her.

“A joint commission,” Queen Isara said. “Two kingdoms, two interests, and perhaps no decision at all. What happens when its representatives disagree?”

Lord Daven inclined his head from the gallery. “A commission would at least put both sides’ evidence before a single table. That is better than leaving every captain to interpret the boundary by cannon range.”

Commander Ash’s expression hardened. “And while the commission debates, Velheim’s ships pass uninspected through waters our patrols are charged to secure.”

Priestess Yuna turned her attention to the Commander. “Then the proposal needs an interim rule. Without one, the dispute continues under the very uncertainty the commission is meant to resolve.”

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. “The court requests clarification on the commission’s authority and interim measures.”

Queen Isara’s gaze returned to you. “Would its findings bind both crowns, Ambassador—or would the commission merely offer advice that either kingdom could ignore?”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet her gaze, my smile unwavering.* "The commission's findings would bind both crowns, Your Majesty. As for interim measures, Velheim proposes all vessels fly a neutral flag while negotiations proceed."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The proposal drew a faint stir through the court. Queen Isara’s fingers rested against the throne’s carved arm, her attention fixed on you.

“Binding findings would give the commission teeth,” she said. “A neutral flag would give it a costume. What would prevent either crown from using that flag to conceal its vessels—or its intentions?”

Commander Ash’s mouth tightened. “Our patrols cannot be expected to trust a banner in place of proper identification. Velheim’s ships would still need to submit to inspection.”

Lord Daven answered before Ash could continue. “Then the interim rule can specify identification and inspection procedures. That is precisely the sort of question a joint commission could settle, provided both crowns agree to abide by its decision.”

“Provided the procedures are known in advance,” Priestess Yuna said. Her voice remained calm. “A neutral flag without shared rules would invite suspicion, not prevent conflict.”

The Herald struck the floor once with his staff. “The court requests the proposed inspection procedure and the means by which the commission’s binding findings would be enforced.”

Queen Isara inclined her head, granting the request without softening her gaze. “The court will not accept a symbol in place of safeguards, Ambassador. What enforcement does Velheim propose if either crown rejects a finding—or if a patrol stops a vessel that has complied with the agreed rules?”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "I have proof." I pull out the intercepted orders and hand them to Priestess Yuna — not the Queen, not the Commander. Yuna. I want a neutral party to read them first.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The intercepted orders passed into Priestess Yuna’s hands. She examined the seals before unfolding the pages, then read them in silence. The court watched her rather than the papers.

Commander Ash stepped forward. “Those documents were taken from the Admiralty’s files. Their presence here proves nothing about their authenticity.”

“Nor does your objection disprove them,” Lord Daven replied. His voice remained smooth, but the edge had returned. “Let the court hear what they say.”

Priestess Yuna finished reading and looked up. “The orders concern the patrols and the stopped vessels. I can attest that the document bears the marks it claims to bear. I cannot, from the seals alone, establish who authorized it or whether this copy has been altered.”

Queen Isara held out her hand. “Then the court will examine the original marks and compare them with the Admiralty’s records.”

The Herald struck the floor. “The intercepted orders are entered for examination by the court.”

Ash’s gaze remained fixed on the documents. “Until their source is established, they are an accusation dressed as evidence.”

“Then the Admiralty’s records should settle the matter,” Queen Isara said. Her eyes returned to you. “The court will not decide the pact on an unverified paper. But the orders are now part of the hearing—and Commander Ash will answer for them once they have been authenticated.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I smile, a flicker of triumph in my eyes.* "Indeed, Your Majesty. I believe the Admiralty's records will prove most illuminating." *I glance pointedly at Commander Ash.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Commander Ash’s gaze met the pointed look, then shifted to the Queen. “The Admiralty’s records will show the order was lawful,” he said. “They will also show why the patrols acted.”

“Then there should be no cause to delay their examination,” Lord Daven replied. “The court deserves the complete record—not a summary selected by the officer under scrutiny.”

Ash’s jaw tightened. “I am not under scrutiny for enforcing a royal order.”

“Not yet,” Queen Isara said. Her voice cut off the rising murmur. “The orders will be compared with the Admiralty’s records before this court draws conclusions. No page will be withheld, and no patrol captain’s account will substitute for the written record.”

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. “By order of Her Majesty, the Admiralty’s records concerning the blockade and inspection protocols will be presented to the court.”

Priestess Yuna lowered the intercepted pages. “The seals can be compared. So can the wording and marks of authorization. That may establish whether this copy matches the official record. It will not, by itself, establish whether the order was just.”

“Justice is not the question before us,” Ash said.

“It has become the question,” the Queen answered, “the moment the blockade became part of a proposed treaty.”

Her gaze settled on you. “The records will be examined. Until then, the court will neither accept Velheim’s terms nor dismiss them. If the documents support your accusation, Ambassador, the court will expect Velheim’s proposed commission to address the authority behind the blockade—not merely the waters where it occurred.”

Lord Daven inclined his head. “A necessary distinction, Your Majesty.”

Queen Isara’s expression remained cold. “The hearing will continue when the records arrive.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I give a slight bow, a confident glint in my eyes.* "As you wish, Your Majesty. Velheim is confident the truth will be clear."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The court’s silence held until the great doors opened. The Herald announced the arrival of the Admiralty’s records, and two attendants carried a locked chest to the foot of the throne.

Queen Isara gestured for it to be opened. “The complete file,” she said. “Here, before the court.”

Commander Ash’s expression stayed rigid as the records were laid out. “The patrols acted under emergency authority. The file will confirm it.”

Priestess Yuna compared the intercepted orders with the official pages. She checked the seals, then followed the lines of authorization with one finger. “The intercepted copy matches the Admiralty record,” she said. “The wording and marks are consistent.”

A murmur stirred through the chamber.

“Then the authenticity is settled,” Lord Daven said. “The authority behind the order is not.”

Yuna turned to the final page. “There is no royal countersignature. The order bears Commander Ash’s authorization.”

Ash’s hand left his sword pommel. “The Admiralty delegated emergency authority to the patrol commander. The situation required immediate action.”

Queen Isara’s eyes narrowed. “The court has received no such delegation.”

“It was issued through the Admiralty,” Ash replied. “The fleet could not wait for a hearing while Velheim’s captains refused inspection.”

“Yet the order continued for six weeks,” Daven said. “An emergency that lasts that long begins to resemble policy.”

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. “The court recognizes the Queen.”

Isara rose from the throne. Her gaze rested on the official records, then shifted to Ash. “The documents establish that the blockade was not ordered by the crown. Commander, name the authority that granted you power to impose it—and produce the delegation.”

Ash’s jaw tightened. “The delegation is in the Admiralty’s files.”

“Then it will be produced,” Isara said. “Until it is, this court will treat the blockade as an order issued in your name, not the crown’s.”

Yuna folded her hands. “That finding should be entered alongside the records. It bears directly on the commission’s jurisdiction.”

Queen Isara looked toward you. “Ambassador, Velheim proposed binding findings between both crowns. The court now asks whether Velheim would accept the same principle here: that a commander’s emergency claim must be reviewed by the joint commission, even when that review could rule against Velheim.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I pause, considering this turn of events. My initial triumph fades slightly.* "Your Majesty, Velheim would accept such a review, provided the commission's authority is absolute and its decisions are final for both kingdoms."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Queen Isara studied you for a measured silence. “Absolute authority is a generous phrase when it is offered by the party seeking redress. It is less generous when the commission rules against that party.”

Lord Daven inclined his head. “Velheim has accepted the risk of an adverse ruling. The court should now decide whether the same standard protects both crowns—or merely restrains them.”

Commander Ash gave a hard, humorless smile. “A foreign commission deciding where our patrols may sail is not review. It is surrender dressed in legal language.”

Priestess Yuna’s gaze remained on the records. “Then the commission’s jurisdiction must be written plainly. It should distinguish unlawful orders from lawful patrols, and emergency action from a prolonged blockade.”

“The court will not surrender its authority by accepting a treaty,” Queen Isara said. “Nor will it permit the crown to promise what it cannot enforce.” Her eyes returned to you. “If the commission’s decisions are final, both kingdoms must agree on its composition, its procedures, and the consequences of defiance.”

The Herald struck the floor once. “The court requests terms governing the commission’s appointment and enforcement.”

Queen Isara’s expression remained cool. “The Admiralty’s delegation will be produced and examined. After that, the court will consider whether this commission can judge the blockade—and what limits it must observe.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly.* "Velheim agrees, Your Majesty. Transparency and clear boundaries are essential for any lasting peace."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your slow nod was met by no visible change in Queen Isara’s expression.

“Then the court will require written terms,” she said. “The commission’s membership, its authority, and the consequences of refusing its findings must be stated without ambiguity. Neither crown will be bound by a promise whose limits remain unwritten.”

Lord Daven’s voice carried from the gallery. “A sound beginning, Your Majesty. The delegation should be produced alongside those terms, so the commission’s first task need not be decided in the abstract.”

Commander Ash’s shoulders stiffened. “The Admiralty’s delegation will confirm that the patrols acted within their authority. It should not be treated as grounds to place our fleet under foreign judgment.”

“Nor should emergency authority be allowed to answer every question about what followed,” Priestess Yuna said. Her gaze stayed on the records. “The duration of the blockade belongs in the same account as its cause.”

Queen Isara regarded Ash for a long moment. “The court will examine both. Until then, no conclusion will be entered as fact.”

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. “By order of Her Majesty, the Admiralty will produce the delegation. The proposed commission’s terms will be submitted for review before the hearing resumes.”

The Queen’s attention returned to you. “Velheim’s acceptance has been noted, Ambassador. The court will judge the written terms when they arrive.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I bow my head slightly.* "Very well, Your Majesty. Velheim's terms will be presented swiftly." *I allow a hint of challenge to enter my voice.* "I trust the Admiralty's delegation will be equally prompt."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The challenge hung in the chamber after your words. Commander Ash’s expression hardened, but Queen Isara answered before he could.

“The Admiralty will produce the delegation promptly,” she said. “If it does not, the delay will be entered into the record.”

Ash straightened. “The Admiralty has nothing to conceal. Its papers will arrive when they are assembled.”

“Then assembly should not take long,” Lord Daven said. “The court has already demanded the complete file.”

Priestess Yuna looked from the records to the Queen. “The delegation must be examined against the order itself. A claim of authority is not proof of authority.”

Queen Isara gave a slight nod. “So ordered. The Herald will record that the delegation and Velheim’s proposed terms are both required before the hearing resumes.”

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. “The court records the requirement. The Admiralty will submit its delegation; Velheim will submit the commission’s written terms.”

The Queen’s gaze settled on you. “When both are before the court, the hearing will continue. Until then, the blockade remains under examination—and no party will mistake a promise of speed for a finding of truth.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I give another slight bow.* "Understood, Your Majesty. Velheim looks forward to the truth emerging." *My eyes flicker to Commander Ash, a subtle challenge in my gaze.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You descended the last flight of stairs and the temperature dropped. The passage opened into a chamber that hadn't seen light in a long time — your torch was the first in decades, maybe centuries, and the shadows retreated from it reluctantly.

Dust covered everything. Thick, undisturbed dust. Except for one set of footprints leading from the far entrance to the center of the room, where something had been dragged. The marks ended at a stone slab. The slab had writing on it.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I kneel down to read the writing on the slab, holding the torch close.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
As you held the torch close, the carving emerged from beneath the dust: a line of cramped, angular letters cut deep into the stone.

**WHEN THE LAST BELL HAD SOUNDED,  
THE NAMELESS ONE HAD BEEN TAKEN BELOW.  
THE DOOR HAD OPENED FOR THE LIVING,  
AND CLOSED UPON THE DEAD.**

Beneath the words, a shallow groove ran across the slab’s edge. The dust there had been disturbed recently—or at least, far more recently than the rest of the chamber. The drag marks ended at the slab’s near side, where a dark seam traced its outline.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: "Nameless One, huh?" I trace the groove with a finger. *I wonder what was dragged here.* I stand up and kick at the dust near the seam.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your boot sent a fan of dust skittering across the stone. Beneath it, a narrow iron ring lay recessed in the groove, black with age except where recent fingers—or something else—had scraped it clean.

The kick also stirred the slab. A faint grinding shudder traveled through the floor, and the dark seam widened by the breadth of a fingernail. Cold air slipped through the gap, carrying the smell of wet earth.

From somewhere below came a single, muffled clang. A bell, sounded once.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I grab the amulet and put it on. Then I turn to face the guardian.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
As the amulet settled against your chest, its metal turned colder than the chamber air. A thin line of blue light traced its worn markings, then guttered to a faint pulse.

Across the slab, the guardian emerged from the shadow beside the far entrance: a tall figure in corroded armor, its face hidden behind a featureless iron mask. Dust slid from its shoulders as it lifted a long, hooked blade. The footprints ended at its feet.

The slab shuddered again. Beneath it, the bell rang a second time—and the guardian’s mask tilted toward the amulet.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: "Well, that's not good." *I grip the hilt of my sword, drawing it from its sheath with a soft rasp of metal.* "You're a little late to the party, aren't you, friend?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your words carried through the chamber. The guardian’s mask remained fixed on the amulet, and its hooked blade lowered by a fraction.

“The bell had called the dead,” it rasped. “The living had no place below.”

A third clang shuddered up through the slab. The iron ring jerked in its groove, and the seam widened enough for a thread of blue light to spill across the dust. The guardian stepped between you and the opening, blade angled toward your chest.

The amulet pulsed once against you. Beneath the stone, something answered with a slow, hollow scrape.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I talk to the ghost. "What happened here? Who are you?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The guardian’s mask dipped, and the hooked blade lowered until its point nearly touched the stone.

“The name was taken from the one dragged below,” it rasped. “The body crossed the threshold. The door closed upon the dead.”

The blue light beneath the slab flickered. The guardian’s gauntlet tightened around its weapon.

“The keeper had no name either,” it continued. “Only a charge: to bar the living from following.”

A fourth bell rang below. The iron ring leapt in its groove, and the slab shifted another finger’s width. For an instant, a pale shape pressed against the gap from underneath.

The guardian turned its mask toward you again.

“The amulet had opened the way,” it said. “Put it aside—or join the nameless below.”

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: "Easy, friend. No need to get your rusted armor in a twist." *I glance at the pale shape, then back at the guardian.* "Is 'Nameless Below' a club? Because I'm not really looking for new memberships right now."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your quip echoed off the chamber walls. The guardian’s mask tilted a fraction, as if it had weighed your words and found them wanting.

“There had been no club,” it rasped. “Only a name. Only a door.”

The pale shape beneath the slab pressed harder against the gap. A thin hand slipped through, its fingers scraping over the stone toward the iron ring. The amulet’s blue pulse quickened against your chest.

The guardian’s hooked blade rose again. “The name had called. The dead had answered.” Its masked face turned toward the slab. “If the door opened, nothing below would remain nameless.”

The ring began to turn by itself. Somewhere beneath the stone, the bell drew a breath of silence before its next strike.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *I grip my sword tighter, my eyes darting between the guardian and the hand reaching for the ring.* "Okay, so no club. Got it. But what *is* this Nameless One? And why is it so eager to get out?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The guardian’s blade held between you and the slab. The pale fingers curled around the iron ring, and the stone groaned beneath their touch.

“The Nameless One had been a keeper,” it rasped. “A name had been cut from the living, and the keeper had carried it below. The body had followed. The door had closed.”

The amulet’s blue pulse quickened against your chest. Beneath the slab, the hand drew the ring another inch.

“It had wanted its name returned,” the guardian said. “The bell had called it. The amulet had answered.”

A fifth clang shuddered through the chamber. The slab lurched, and a cold breath spilled over your boots. The guardian turned its blank mask toward you.

“If it crossed the threshold,” it rasped, “the name would have belonged to it again.” Its blade rose. “And the living who heard it would have been called by name.”

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: "So it's a game of keep-away, huh?" *I shift my weight, preparing to move.* "And now it wants *my* name? Not a chance."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The guardian’s mask turned toward you. Its blade flashed—not toward your sword, but toward the amulet at your throat.

The slab lurched. The pale hand hauled the iron ring another inch, and blue light spilled across the chamber floor. From beneath the stone came a whisper that shaped itself around the sound of your breathing, searching for a name it could claim.

The guardian’s hooked blade swept within reach of the amulet’s chain. “The name had been taken,” it rasped. “The door had to remain closed.”

A sixth bell began to toll below. The guardian’s strike was still coming, and the hand beneath the slab tightened around the ring.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *I duck under the blade, moving closer to the slab, my sword ready.* "I don't think so, pal. No one's taking anything from me."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You ducked beneath the guardian’s sweeping blade and closed the distance to the slab. The hook caught the amulet’s chain as it passed; metal snapped, and the amulet struck the stone near your boots, its blue light flaring bright enough to throw every shadow against the walls.

The guardian’s blade crashed into the slab’s edge. Stone chipped, and the iron ring wrenched beneath the pale hand’s grip. The sixth bell finished tolling below.

For a heartbeat, the whisper beneath the slab fell silent. Then it spoke from the widening gap—not in words, but in the sound of a name almost remembered. The amulet pulsed again on the floor. The guardian staggered, its blank mask turning toward it.

“The name had heard you,” it rasped. Its hooked blade scraped across the stone as it turned back toward you. “Do not let it answer.”

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: "Heard me? What are you talking about?" *I kick the amulet further away from the gap, then bring my sword up to parry.* "And what exactly is a 'name' that I shouldn't let answer?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your kick sent the amulet skidding across the stone, away from the gap. Its blue light thinned to a wavering thread, and the whisper beneath the slab broke into a hiss.

The guardian’s hooked blade struck your raised sword with a clang that jolted up your arms. It did not press the attack. Instead, it held the crossed weapons between you and the slab, its mask angled toward the amulet.

“A name was more than a word,” it rasped. “It had bound the living to the self they had been. The Nameless One had lost that bond—and sought to take another.”

The pale hand tightened around the iron ring. The slab dragged another fraction open, and cold air poured through the widening seam.

“The amulet had carried the missing name’s call,” the guardian said. “When the thing below heard a living voice answer, it could claim that voice in return.”

A seventh bell stirred somewhere beneath you, its first note trembling in the stone. The guardian’s blade shuddered against yours. Beyond it, the hand began pulling the ring again.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: "So it's trying to steal my identity, basically?" *I push back against its blade, trying to disengage.* "Not on my watch, pal."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your push forced the guardian’s hooked blade sideways. The weapons separated with a shriek of metal, and the guardian stumbled one step toward the slab before catching its balance.

“Yes,” it rasped. “It had wanted the self beneath the name.”

The seventh bell struck. The note rolled through the chamber, and the pale hand beneath the slab clenched around the ring. The stone dragged open another inch. A voice spilled through the gap, whispering the shape of a name—almost yours, but not quite.

The guardian froze. Blue light flared beneath its mask, and its blade dipped toward the floor.

Across the chamber, the amulet gave one faint pulse. The whisper sharpened, reaching toward you. The guardian turned its mask to you again.

“Do not answer,” it said. “Not even to deny it.”

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *I ignore the guardian, staring at the gap.* The whisper… it’s so close to my name. "What happens if I don't answer?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot. The forge crackled behind him. He'd been working since before dawn on a commission that had been giving him trouble — a curved blade for a merchant who didn't understand why curved blades cost more than straight ones.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum’s jaw tightened. He glanced toward the door, then back to the troublesome blade.

“Urgent,” he said. “Nobles call all things urgent when coin is theirs. Tell him Grum is at work. If he wants forge time, he can wait till blade is done.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, hefting the coal bucket again. It's heavy.* "He sounds pretty important, Grum. And mad. He's wearing a really fancy cape."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum’s eyes narrowed at mention of fancy cape. He hung rag on an iron hook and turned back to blade.

“Cape can wait,” he said. “Tell him Grum will see him when blade is done. If he steps in forge, call Grum.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum set down hammer and turned toward door. His gaze held steady on noble.

“You want sword by dawn? No. Good steel takes time. Grum will not rush work for silk cape. Pay fair, wait till blade is done, or go.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince, shrinking back a little from Grum's tone. The noble looks like he's about to explode.* "Uh, Grum, maybe I should just tell him you're busy with another customer?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum’s gaze softened as he saw Apprentice shrink back. He stepped between them and the door.

“Good. Tell him Grum has work to do. You stay by forge. Grum will deal with silk cape.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod quickly, relieved, and scurry back to the coal pile.* "Okay, Grum. You got it." *I start shoveling coal, trying to look busy.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum glanced back toward the forge, making sure Apprentice stayed clear of the door. Then he faced the noble, broad shoulders set between him and the work.

“Keep coal fed. Grum has this.”

The noble’s face had gone red beneath his fine hat. Grum did not shift an inch.

“Silk cape can shout. Steel will not bend for it. No sword by dawn. Pay fair, wait, or leave.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I accidentally burn my hand badly on the forge. I cry out in pain.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum spun from the noble at the cry. His anger vanished; he crossed the forge in two strides, putting himself between Apprentice and the fire.

“Move, cape. Give room.” His voice cut through the forge’s roar. “Apprentice, hand under cool water. Now. Grum will get clean cloth.”

He reached for the water pail, then stopped short of touching the burned hand. His face had gone grim with worry.

“Keep hand cool. No ice. Grum has you.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I'm holding my hand under the pump, hissing in pain.* "It really stings, Grum! I think I messed up bad."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum’s face tightened with worry. He stayed close, careful not to touch the burned skin, and checked that cool water kept running over it.

“Keep hand under cool water for twenty min. No ice. No grease. Take off rings if they come free,” he said. “Burn on hand needs healer to check. Grum will get one now.”

He turned on the noble, voice hard.

“Silk cape, fetch town healer. Run.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I pull my hand out of the water for a second to look at it, then quickly put it back, wincing.* "Twenty minutes? That's a long time. It really hurts."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum stayed beside the pump, keeping his hands clear of the burn. His brow furrowed, but his voice softened.

“Grum knows it hurts. Keep hand in cool flow for twenty min. Do not pull it out to look. Cool water helps. Grum will stay here till healer comes.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I try to keep my hand under the water, but it's really hard. I'm shaking a little.* "Is it going to scar, Grum? Will I still be able to hold a hammer?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum crouched beside the pump, his face still tight with worry. He kept his voice low and steady.

“Grum cannot tell yet. Some burns heal well; deep burn can scar or make grip weak for a time. Healer needs to see it soon. Do not test hand with hammer.”

He glanced toward the door, then back to the running water.

“Keep it cool for full twenty min. Grum will stay here. You will not face this alone.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, trying to focus on the cool water, but my vision is a little blurry.* "Okay... okay, Grum." *I lean against the pump, trying not to cry.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum saw Apprentice’s sight go unfixed and moved close, ready to catch them if their knees gave way. He kept the burned hand beneath cool water.

“Apprentice, sit down slow. Do not stand. Grum will keep you safe.”

He turned his head toward the door, voice sharp as struck iron.

“Cape! Get healer now. Tell them hand burn, and sight gone blurry. Run!”

Grum stayed at Apprentice’s side, watching their face as the water ran.

“Keep hand cool. Do not look at burn. Grum is here.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I try to sit, but my legs feel like jelly. I slide down the side of the pump, still keeping my hand in the water. My head feels a little swimmy.* "It's so dizzy, Grum."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum dropped to one knee beside Apprentice, one arm ready to steady them without touching burned skin. His face went pale beneath the soot.

“Do not stand. Stay low. Grum has you.” He called toward the door, voice hard. “Cape! Get healer now. Tell them Apprentice feels faint and has bad hand burn. Run!”

Grum tugged a clean cloth around Apprentice’s shoulders, keeping it well clear of the burn, then watched their face.

“Keep hand in cool flow. Do not let rest of you get cold. Grum will stay.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I shiver, despite the cloth. My teeth are chattering a little.* "My head hurts, Grum. Everything's really loud."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's office was above a dry cleaner's on Mercer Street. It smelled faintly of chemicals and coffee that had been reheated too many times. She kept the blinds half-closed — enough light to work, not enough for anyone on the street to see in clearly.

She opened the case file the client had brought. Spread the photos across the desk. Looked at them for a long time without saying anything.

"The last person to investigate this was a detective at the Ninth Precinct." She closed the file. "That's a problem."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Why is that a problem? Can't we just go talk to them? The Ninth Precinct is twenty minutes from here."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content: Lena’s expression stayed unreadable. “Because if the precinct has a file, asking questions there could tip someone off before we know what they’ve recorded.” She slid one photo back into the folder. “I’ll contact the detective somewhere else, or find the paper trail first. We won’t need to go inside.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "You think they're hiding something?" I leaned forward, my voice dropping. "Is that what you're saying?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena held the client’s gaze for a moment, then squared the edges of the photographs.

“I’m saying we don’t know what they recorded—or who’s seen it.” Her voice stayed even. “That isn’t proof anyone’s hiding something. It’s a reason not to announce our questions before we know what to ask.”

She set the folder aside. “I’ll find the detective somewhere off-site. Until then, I’ll trace the paper trail.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Lena, were you a cop? You talk about this stuff like someone who's been on the inside."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena’s gaze settled on the closed folder.

“Experience comes from asking the wrong questions and watching what people do with them,” she said. “The useful question now is who had access to that file after the investigation stopped.”

She pulled a notepad toward her and wrote down the detective’s name. “I’ll start there.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Okay. So, what do you need from me? Should I try to dig up anything on the detective?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena turned the notepad so the detective’s name faced the client.

“Look for public records tied to the case—its number, the dates it was active, and any notices or correspondence you already have. If you find the detective’s current contact information, note where it came from. Don’t contact them yet; I want to know what we’re asking before we make ourselves memorable.”

She slid the folder back across the desk. “And bring me anything you find, even if it seems routine. Small details tend to be the ones people forget to explain.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Got it. No calls, just research." I picked up the folder. "I'll start digging tonight."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena tapped the edge of the notepad once.

“Use public sources only. Don’t try to get into anyone’s account or pull favors from someone with access. If you find a case number or a date that doesn’t fit, write down exactly where you found it.”

She tucked the detective’s name beneath the folder’s cover. “And keep copies of anything you bring me. I’d rather not have the only record disappear.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "The witness says the detective who worked this case was named Torres. Detective M. Torres. Does that name mean anything to you?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena’s fingers paused on the folder’s edge. Whatever she made of the name, she gave nothing away.

“Torres is common enough that I won’t treat it as confirmation,” she said. “We’ll need the first initial, the case number, or something tying that detective to this specific investigation.”

She wrote **M. Torres** beneath the date on her notepad. “Ask the witness when they heard the name and whether they saw it on a document. Don’t press them for a theory—just the exact detail they remember.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "The witness is dead, Lena. That's why this is a cold case." I said quietly. "Are you forgetting that?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena’s pen stopped.

“No. I gave you an instruction that couldn’t be followed.” She set it down, her expression tightening by a fraction. “You’re right.”

She drew a line through the note about asking the witness. “Then we work from what survived: the original statement, any notes or transcript, and the date it was recorded. If the name came through someone else, I want to know who relayed it and whether they were quoting a document or repeating what they’d heard.”

Her gaze returned to the folder. “We don’t fill gaps with guesses. We find the source of the name.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Okay. I'll see what I can find. I'll focus on the original documents, try to track down where 'M. Torres' first appeared." *I nodded, understanding the gravity of her words.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena gave a short nod and wrote **M. Torres** beside the case date.

“Start with the earliest surviving copy—not a summary someone made later. Note where it came from, who kept it, and whether the name was handwritten, typed, or added afterward.” She capped her pen. “Don’t annotate the original. Photograph it or make a copy, and keep the source with it.”

She tucked the notepad beneath the folder. “I’ll look for the case number through public records. If the name appears in more than one place, we’ll compare the dates before deciding what it means.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Got it. Earliest surviving copy. No annotations." I paused. "So, you're not going to try and find other detectives named Torres?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content: “Not yet,” Lena said. She kept the pen beside the case file. “A list of people named Torres would give us more noise, not better evidence. First we establish whether M. Torres appears in the earliest records and what role the name was attached to. If that points to a specific person, I’ll verify it through public sources before making contact.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Makes sense. We're looking for *this* Torres, not just *a* Torres." I picked up the folder. "I'll be in touch once I've got something."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena gathered the loose photographs and slid them back into the folder.

“Good. Keep a note of every source you check, including the ones that turn up nothing. And don’t leave the original documents with anyone who can’t account for them.”

She rested one hand on the closed file. “I’ll trace the case number through public records. When you have the earliest copy, bring me the source along with it.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Will do." *I gave a slight nod, then headed for the door.* "I'll call you when I have something worth looking at."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena waited until the office had gone quiet before opening the folder again. The photographs lay in a neat stack beside her notepad; **M. Torres** remained the only name she had.

She checked the documents for a case number, a date, anything that could narrow a public-records search. There was nothing she trusted enough to treat as a lead. She wrote down the gaps instead, then opened the city archive’s online index and began with the case date.

When the search returned no useful match, she noted that too. A blank result wasn’t proof of anything—but it told her which records office to ask next. She drafted a request for the public index, careful to ask for the case number and document dates, not for anyone’s theory about what had happened.

Then she set the draft beside the folder and marked it **HOLD: confirm date**.

“First the source,” she murmured, and turned back to the records.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content:
*I spent the next few days holed up in my apartment, cross-referencing everything I had. The name "M. Torres" kept popping up, but always as a secondary reference. Finally, I found it.*

*I called Lena's office, hoping she was there.* "Lena, I think I found him. Or at least, the first mention of him."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The door to The Gilded Antler opened with a creak that Maren kept meaning to oil and kept forgetting. She looked up from the bar, where she was wiping down the counter with her left hand — the right holding a tally sheet she was checking against the evening's orders.

The common room was about half full. Two merchants arguing quietly in the corner about grain prices. A dwarf nursing an ale and reading a letter. Old Pell's venison stew on every other table, filling the room with the smell of rosemary and slow-cooked meat.

Maren set down the tally sheet and gave the newcomer a once-over. Road-dusted. Tired. Carrying something they were being careful with.

"Welcome to the Antler, friend. Sit where you like. Kitchen is open for another hour."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I take a seat at the bar. Set my pack down carefully. "Whatever's hot and a room for the night, if you've got one."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren set the cloth aside and reached for a bowl with her left hand. “We have rooms, friend. The venison stew is hot, and there is bread enough to make it a proper meal.”

She ladled a generous portion from the pot, then glanced toward the stairwell. “I will have a room made ready. One night?”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "One night for now," I reply, my voice a little rough. *I rub my eyes, then look at the stew.* "Smells good."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren set the bowl before them with her left hand, then placed a thick slice of bread beside it. “Old Pell knows his way around a stew pot. He is less reliable with compliments, but the stew has never complained.”

She reached for a clean cup. “Ale, water, or something stronger with it?”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: A merchant at a nearby table sends over a plate as a gesture of goodwill. "Compliments of Lord Havel — fresh crab cakes from the coast, arrived this morning. Finest in the region." The plate is set in front of both of us.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren’s left hand stopped short of the cup. Her gaze settled on the crab cakes, and her expression went politely blank.

“Kind of Lord Havel,” she said. “But I do not care for seafood, and crab beside an open bowl is an invitation for the stew to taste of the coast.”

She lifted two fingers toward one of the servers. “Would you take that back to him, please? Thank him for the thought.”

Then she turned back to the bar, keeping her hands clear of the plate. “Your ale or water, friend?”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I eye the crab cakes, then Maren's face.* "No worries, I'll take 'em off your hands." *I pick up a crab cake and take a bite.* "These are pretty good, actually."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren gave the crab cake a glance, then returned her attention to the cup. “I am glad one of us appreciates them. Keep the plate on your side, friend. That stew has put in a long day without borrowing flavor from the coast.”

She poured the ale with her left hand and set it down well clear of the plate. “I will tell Lord Havel his gift found an appreciative home.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren lifted her own cup with her left hand, keeping well clear of the crab cakes. “To Old Pell. He will pretend not to hear you, then make an extra loaf tomorrow so nobody can accuse him of enjoying praise.”
